title: DTC B0001 - Driver Frontal Stage 1 Deployment Control
problem_description: The supplemental restraint system (SRS) module has detected a fault in the deployment control circuit for the first stage of the driver frontal airbag. The SRS warning lamp illuminates and airbag deployment may be impaired in a crash event.
symptoms: Warning light or symbol related to the affected system
Comfort or safety function impaired
possible_causes: Clock spring (spiral cable) damaged in steering column (likelihood: high)
Loose or corroded airbag connector under steering wheel (likelihood: medium)
SRS control module internal fault (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code B0001 (Driver Frontal Stage 1 Deployment Control).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: driver airbag module, srs control module, srs wiring, clock spring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1.0-4.0 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Clock spring (spiral cable) damaged in steering column (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Loose or corroded airbag connector under steering wheel (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard
preprocessing_notes: Ingested from B0xxx_enriched.yaml; standardized into vehicle troubleshooting schema.

title: DTC B010B - Camera Washer Actuator B
problem_description: Fault on camera washer actuator B. Such an actuator is usually a small solenoid valve or a dedicated pump outlet that releases washer fluid to the nozzle of one camera, for example a rear-view, surround-view or driver-assistance camera; the letter only tells which actuator the manufacturer assigned to which camera. When it fails, that lens can no longer be rinsed on demand, and dirt on it can blur the image or make the systems that rely on the camera switch off.
symptoms: Camera lens is not cleaned when washing is requested
Blurred or obstructed camera image

title: DTC B0117 - Camera Washer Actuator O
problem_description: Fault on camera washer actuator O. Such an actuator is usually a small solenoid valve or a dedicated pump outlet that releases washer fluid to the nozzle of one camera, for example a rear-view, surround-view or driver-assistance camera; the letter only tells which actuator the manufacturer assigned to which camera. When it fails, that lens can no longer be rinsed on demand, and dirt on it can blur the image or make the systems that rely on the camera switch off.
symptoms: Camera lens is not cleaned when washing is requested
Blurred or obstructed camera image
Message that a camera is blocked or a driver-assistance function is unavailable
possible_causes: Washer actuator failed (likelihood: high)
Open or shorted actuator wiring, or corroded connector (likelihood: medium)
Blocked or frozen nozzle or supply hose (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code B0117 (Camera Washer Actuator O).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: camera washer actuator o, actuator wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Washer actuator failed (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Open or shorted actuator wiring, or corroded connector (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC C0001 - TCS Control Channel A Valve 1
problem_description: Covers the first solenoid valve in control channel A of the traction control system, part of the ABS/ESC hydraulic modulator. During a traction event the control module pulses this valve to build and hold brake pressure at a spinning driven wheel without driver pedal input. The module monitors the valve coil circuit for opens, shorts to power or ground and for a resistance outside the expected range, and also checks that commanded and achieved pressure agree. A fault disables traction control and usually the stability function. No manufacturer publishes a code-specific bulletin; the entry follows the SAE J2012 generic definition and the documented operating principle of channel-based ABS modulators.

title: DTC C0002 - TCS Control Channel A Valve 2
problem_description: Covers the second solenoid valve in control channel A of the traction control system. Where valve 1 typically isolates or applies pressure, valve 2 handles the complementary release or dump function so the modulator can both raise and reduce pressure at the controlled wheel during a traction intervention. The control module watches the coil circuit for opens, shorts and out-of-range resistance and verifies that the pressure response matches the command. Detection of a fault sets the ABS lamp and turns off traction and stability control while leaving conventional braking intact. There is no public code-specific service document; the entry reflects the SAE J2012 generic definition and standard two-valve channel modulator design.
symptoms: ABS warning lamp on

title: DTC C0258 - Brake Booster Vacuum Sensor Circuit
problem_description: The brake booster vacuum sensor reports an implausible signal; brake assist functions are reduced. The vacuum sensor tells the brake control module how much vacuum is stored in the booster; with too little vacuum the assist drops, so the module uses the signal to request more vacuum (electric pump or engine intervention) or to add hydraulic brake assist. If power assist is lost, the brakes still work through the master cylinder, but a much higher pedal force is needed.
symptoms: Brake system warning lamp or message
Possible reduced brake assist
Firmer brake pedal, longer pedal travel or higher pedal force
Driver-assistance functions such as automatic emergency braking or adaptive cruise control may be disabled
possible_causes: Vacuum hose leak (likelihood: high)
Sensor failed (likelihood: medium)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code C0258 (Brake Booster Vacuum Sensor Circuit).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: brake booster vacuum sensor, vacuum hose.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Vacuum hose leak (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Sensor failed (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC C0535 - Motor Control B Range/Performance
problem_description: Second motor channel B fails its plausibility check: wiring and supply test fine, yet the motor's reaction to commands is wrong, for example too little speed, a delayed start or no stop. Where a controller drives two motors or two channels, A and B separate them; J2012 does not say which motor B is, and no manufacturer publicly assigns C0535, so the meaning must come from the vehicle's own service data. title: DTC C0536 - Motor Control B Circuit/Open
problem_description: Motor control B finds its load missing. The module expects a closed path through the windings of channel B and sees an open circuit instead – a pulled connector, a cut lead, corroded pins or an internal break in the motor. title: DTC C053A - ABS Valves Missing Calibration
problem_description: The brake control unit holds no valid calibration for its ABS valves. Analog-controlled inlet valves open at a current that depends on the pressure difference, manufacturing scatter and wear, so the controller needs a stored opening-current curve to meter pressure finely. Continental patents describe how it is learned: the pump builds pressure (about 130–150 bar, or points at 150 and 50 bar) against a valve held shut by roughly 1800 mA, then the current is lowered until the valve opens. One of them notes the data are lost when the electronics are replaced. Hence the code typically follows a module or hydraulic unit swap, or an aborted learning run. No manufacturer documents C053A publicly; running the calibration with a scan tool usually clears it.

title: DTC C0554 - Longitudinal Acceleration Sensor Circuit High
problem_description: C0554 is the upper counterpart of C0553: the fore-aft acceleration voltage stays above the highest value that a real sensor reading may take. With a mid-scale zero point, as in a Hyundai/Kia G-sensor patent (2.5 V on a 5 V supply), a value pinned near the reference voltage would mean an absurd, constant acceleration, so the module treats it as a circuit fault. title: DTC C055B - ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage Circuit A Low
problem_description: Supply voltage A of the pump motor is below its lower limit. A patent originally filed by AlliedSignal and now owned by Bosch flags its own fault if the motor sits under roughly 7 V at shut-off, and a Hitachi patent for electric brake actuators limits motor current once the vehicle supply falls under a set level. symptoms: ABS warning light on
ESC/stability control deactivated
Possible reduced brake assist
Speedometer may behave erratically
possible_causes: Control wiring fault (likelihood: high)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code C0632 (Front Axle Disconnect Control Circuit).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: front axle disconnect actuator, control wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-4 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Control wiring fault (likelihood: high).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard
preprocessing_notes: Ingested from C0xxx_enriched.yaml; standardized into vehicle troubleshooting schema.

title: DTC P0001 - Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open
problem_description: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0001 is set when the control module detects that the control circuit of this valve is open, i.e. no plausible current flows when the valve is driven. Rail pressure can then no longer be controlled as intended. Whether the valve is open or closed without current depends on the design, so the same fault can cause excess pressure in one system and no pressure in another.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Engine cranks but does not start, or stalls (normally closed valve)
Loss of power or limp mode (normally open valve)
Additional rail pressure codes possible
possible_causes: Connector at the regulator loose, corroded or unplugged (likelihood: high)
Solenoid coil of the regulator open (likelihood: medium)
Broken wire in the harness, e.g. chafing or rodent damage (likelihood: medium)
Output driver in the engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0001 (Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel volume regulator, high pressure fuel pump, fuel volume regulator wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Connector at the regulator loose, corroded or unplugged (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Solenoid coil of the regulator open (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P001A - A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
problem_description: A camshaft profile actuator switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between two or more fixed cam profiles with different valve lift and duration, for example by shifting a cam piece axially or by locking rocker arms or tappets with oil pressure. Unlike a camshaft phaser it does not shift the timing continuously. The second letter "A" in the title numbers the actuator on this camshaft. This code is set when the control circuit of the actuator is open: no current flows when it is driven, because of a broken wire, an unplugged connector or an open coil. The engine usually stays on one profile, typically the base profile with low lift. Some manufacturers report these faults with their own codes instead.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Less power at high engine speed because the profile does not switch
Higher consumption or uneven part-load running, depending on the profile
Engine speed may be limited
possible_causes: Connector at the actuator corroded, oil-soaked or loose (likelihood: high)
Wire broken, e.g. at the valve cover (likelihood: medium)
Actuator coil open (likelihood: medium)
Output driver in the engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P001A (A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: camshaft profile actuator intake bank1, camshaft profile actuator wiring, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.

problem_description: The engine control module compares the commanded position of the intake camshaft on bank 2 with the actual position from the camshaft and crankshaft sensors. This code is set when the camshaft stays further retarded than commanded for longer than a calibrated time. Usually the phaser does not move far enough out of its rest position, because oil pressure is too low to release the locking pin, the oil control valve does not open, or the oil screen is blocked. A stretched timing chain also shifts the camshaft towards retarded. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines; it is the cylinder bank without cylinder 1.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Noticeably less torque and pulling power
Higher fuel consumption
Harder starting in some cases
Rattle from the timing drive if the chain is stretched
possible_causes: Oil pressure or oil level too low, oil worn out (likelihood: high)
Oil control valve sticking closed or its screen blocked (likelihood: high)
Cam phaser defective or seized in its rest position (likelihood: medium)
Timing chain stretched or jumped a tooth (likelihood: medium)
Wear debris in the oil circuit, e.g. from a thrust bearing (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0022 ("A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Retarded (Bank 2)).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: cam phaser intake bank2, oil control valve intake bank2, engine oil, timing chain.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-10 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Oil pressure or oil level too low, oil worn out (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Oil control valve sticking closed or its screen blocked (likelihood: high).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P0023 - "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Circuit (Bank 2)
problem_description: The engine control module drives the oil control valve (a pulse-width modulated solenoid) of the variable valve timing on the exhaust camshaft on bank 2. It checks the electrical state of this output and sets the code when the circuit is open, or when the measured state does not match the command, for example because of a short. Camshaft adjustment is then disabled and the phaser stays in its locked rest position: the engine keeps running, but with less torque and higher consumption. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines; it is the cylinder bank without cylinder 1.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Less pulling power at low and medium engine speed
Rough idle in some engines
Slightly higher fuel consumption
possible_causes: Solenoid coil of the oil control valve open or shorted (likelihood: high)
Connector corroded, loose or soaked with engine oil wicking through the valve (likelihood: high)
Wiring harness chafed through or broken (likelihood: medium)
Supply voltage missing, e.g. blown fuse (likelihood: medium)
Output driver in the engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0023 ("B" Camshaft Position Actuator Circuit (Bank 2)).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: oil control valve exhaust bank2, oil control valve wiring, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Solenoid coil of the oil control valve open or shorted (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Connector corroded, loose or soaked with engine oil wicking through the valve (likelihood: high).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P0026 - Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
problem_description: A solenoid valve routes engine oil to a valve control element on the intake side of bank 1. Depending on the manufacturer this is a valve lift changeover or a camshaft phaser. P0026 is a plausibility fault: the electrical control is in order, but the expected effect does not occur or comes too late. The control module recognises this from feedback such as an oil pressure switch or the camshaft sensor. Pure circuit faults of the same solenoid have their own codes. The engine usually remains drivable, but with less power and higher consumption.

Loss of power, no extra pull at higher engine speed
Higher fuel consumption
Rough idle possible if a phaser is affected

Feedback oil pressure switch faulty or leaking (systems with switch) (likelihood: high)
Screen in front of the solenoid clogged, or solenoid sticking (likelihood: medium)
Mechanical fault in the valve train, e.g. locking pin or phaser sticking (likelihood: medium)
Contact resistance in wiring or connector (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: valve control solenoid intake bank1, engine oil, oil pressure switch, valve train.

title: DTC P002A - B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
problem_description: A camshaft profile actuator switches the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) on bank 1 between two or more fixed cam profiles with different valve lift and duration, for example by shifting a cam piece axially or by locking rocker arms or tappets with oil pressure. Unlike a camshaft phaser it does not shift the timing continuously. The second letter "A" in the title numbers the actuator on this camshaft. This code is set when the control circuit of the actuator is open: no current flows when it is driven, because of a broken wire, an unplugged connector or an open coil. The engine usually stays on one profile, typically the base profile with low lift. Some manufacturers report these faults with their own codes instead.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Less power at high engine speed because the profile does not switch
Higher consumption or uneven part-load running, depending on the profile
Engine speed may be limited
possible_causes: Connector at the actuator corroded, oil-soaked or loose (likelihood: high)
Wire broken, e.g. at the valve cover (likelihood: medium)
Actuator coil open (likelihood: medium)
Output driver in the engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: camshaft profile actuator exhaust bank1, camshaft profile actuator wiring, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.

title: DTC P0030 - HO2S Heater Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
problem_description: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) only delivers a usable signal once its ceramic element is hot. A heating element inside the sensor gets it there quickly after a cold start. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse or relay, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while comparing the commanded state with the measured voltage or current. P0030 is the general circuit fault: the measured state does not fit the command, most often because the circuit is interrupted. Which physical fault sets P0030, P0031 or P0032 is defined by each manufacturer. Without heating, closed-loop mixture control starts late and cold-start emissions rise.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable drivability problem
Closed-loop control starts late after a cold start
Emissions test or readiness check failed
possible_causes: Heater circuit interrupted, e.g. broken or chafed wire near the exhaust (likelihood: high)
Heating element inside the sensor burnt out (likelihood: high)
Connector corroded or terminal pushed back (likelihood: medium)

title: DTC P003A - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
problem_description: The electric boost actuator A positions the variable turbine vanes or the wastegate and reports its position through a sensor. In a learning run, for example with the engine warm at idle or after switching off, the control module drives the actuator to its mechanical end stops and stores the sensor values as reference. P003A is set when a learned end position or the total travel lies outside the permitted limits. Typical reasons are worn or sticking vanes or linkage, a faulty actuator, a broken actuator lever, or a replacement actuator that has not been learned in. A usually denotes the first turbocharger in the exhaust flow.

title: DTC P003C - A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
problem_description: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.

title: DTC P005A - B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
problem_description: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.

title: DTC P0065 - Air Assisted Injector Control Range/Performance
problem_description: Air-assisted injectors have an air sleeve around the nozzle tip: air flowing past at high speed breaks the fuel spray into finer droplets, which improves combustion and cold starts and lowers hydrocarbon emissions. The system is rare and mainly found on older engines. P0065 means the control is electrically in order, but the effect is implausible. One documented method compares the idle speed controller correction with the air assistance switched on and off during stable idle; if the difference is too large, the code is set.

title: DTC P006D - Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 1
problem_description: Without boost, for example with the engine stopped or at low load, the pressure sensor ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger must read about the same as the barometric pressure sensor. title: DTC P0090 - Fuel Pressure Regulator A Control Circuit/Open
problem_description: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. Some manufacturers report the pump valve under the "fuel volume regulator" codes instead. P0090 is the general circuit fault, usually an open circuit: the driver voltage or current does not fit the command. title: DTC P009F - Fuel Pressure Relief Control Stuck On
problem_description: The fuel pressure relief control is an electrically controlled valve on the fuel rail that the engine control module opens to reduce rail pressure deliberately, for example on overrun, on load drops or when the engine is switched off. Manufacturer bulletins name internal leakage of this valve as a known fault; low rail pressure codes often appear at the same time.

title: DTC P00AF - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Module Performance
problem_description: Boost control A here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. P00AF is set when actuator A reports such an internal fault. Manufacturer bulletins recommend checking the vane mechanism for free movement and, if it moves freely, replacing only the actuator rather than the whole turbocharger.
symptoms: Check engine light on

title: DTC P00D1 - HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
problem_description: This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor upstream of the catalytic converter (sensor 1) on bank 1. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit. For this sensor position no manufacturer description of the test was found; the code appears in a manufacturer's code list, and the explanation follows the documented counterpart for sensor 2.

Oxygen sensor heater readiness stays incomplete

Too low supply voltage at the sensor connector, e.g. poor ground (likelihood: medium)
Diagnostic software (manufacturer updates exist for some vehicles) (likelihood: medium)
Replacement sensor with a different heater (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P00D5 - HO2S Sensor Correlation Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 1 Sensor 2
problem_description: During fuel cut-off on overrun the exhaust gas is pure air, so the oxygen sensors before and behind the catalytic converter must both report the same lean value. title: DTC P00E3 - Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Stuck Open
problem_description: Some engines, mainly hybrids and fuel-saving designs, have an exhaust heat exchanger behind the catalytic converter that transfers exhaust heat into the coolant for faster warm-up of engine and cabin. A bypass valve sends the exhaust either through the heat exchanger or around it. Documented diagnostics compare the coolant temperature rise at the heat exchanger with the commanded mode: if it behaves like bypass while recovery is commanded, or the other way round, the valve is considered stuck. P00E3 reports the valve stuck open. How "open" and "closed" map to bypass and recovery is not publicly documented, so both possible effects should be considered: slow warm-up and weak heating, or excessive coolant heat. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

title: DTC P00FE - EVAP System Tank Vapor Line Restricted/Blocked
problem_description: The evaporative emission system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister and later purges it into the engine. P00FE means the vapour path between tank and canister is restricted or blocked. That matters because a blocked line can hide the tank side from the leak test and disturb tank venting and refuelling. Ford, where P00FE replaces its own code P144A, checks this once per drive cycle during the cruise leak test, while purging with the vent valve closed, and confirms suspicious pressure responses with an intrusive test. VW used the same code on the 2013–2019 Golf, where the diagnosis covers the purge valve and the leak detection module. Typical causes are kinked or pinched lines and charcoal grains from a broken canister.

title: DTC P0100 - Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit
problem_description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0100 means the control module gets no usable signal at all. Ford uses it for a broken sensing element on digital sensors (period longer than 1.3 ms, i.e. below about 0.78 kHz, for half a second); on GM's 3.0 V6 in the Saab 9-4X it is set at 0 Hz. Many systems with voltage sensors skip P0100 and report low or high directly. The engine then runs on air mass calculated from manifold pressure, throttle angle and speed; Ford also disables start-stop.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value)
Hard starting or stalling
Higher fuel consumption
possible_causes: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open (likelihood: high)
Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics) (likelihood: high)
Supply fuse or relay failed (likelihood: medium)
Control module input faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0100 (Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: mass air flow sensor, mass air flow sensor wiring, sensor supply voltage.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics) (likelihood: high).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P0101 - Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
problem_description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0101 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the engine's state. GM petrol engines model the expected air flow from manifold pressure, throttle, speed and boost and blame the MAF if it is off by more than 20 g/s; GM diesels check the measured-to-estimated ratio (0.8–1.2) with EGR closed; Bosch ME9 compares it with the throttle angle. Common causes are air leaks after the sensor, a soiled element (oiled sport filters) or a disconnected crankcase vent; GM also documents a bad crimp in the fuse box. Ford uses P0068 instead. Two trips are needed.

Hesitation, flat spot, poor throttle response
Rough idle or stalling
Higher consumption, often with lean codes P0171/P0174

Contaminated sensing element (oil from oiled sport filter, dust) (likelihood: high)
Leaking or disconnected crankcase ventilation (likelihood: medium)
Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake (likelihood: medium)
Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring (likelihood: medium)

title: DTC P0105 - Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit
problem_description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0105 is the general circuit fault and is rarely used today: most petrol engines report low, high and intermittent separately (P0107–P0109). It appears mainly where the fault cannot be broken down further – Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the digital SENT sensor reports a bad status or an out-of-limit value for 5 s (lost communication is a separate U code), and Bosch EDC16 diesels use it with a fault type byte, for example signal below 0.2 V. Saab then substitutes 101.3 kPa, limits torque and switches off EGR and boost control.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit (diesel)
Rough idle, hard starting, higher consumption (petrol)
Smoke possible on diesels
possible_causes: Connector or wiring to the sensor open, shorted or loose (likelihood: high)
MAP sensor faulty (oiled, failed internally, SENT status fault) (likelihood: medium)
Sensor hose disconnected, vacuum or boost leak (likelihood: medium)
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same circuit (likelihood: low)
Engine control module faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: manifold absolute pressure sensor, sensor wiring, sensor reference voltage.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

title: DTC P0125 - Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Closed Loop Fuel Control

title: DTC P0127 - Intake Air Temperature Too High
problem_description: P0127 is not a circuit fault but a functional check of the air path: the measured intake air temperature is too high for the operating state. The logic is documented for a Bosch EDC16 diesel (Saab 9-3): if the intake air exceeds 130 °C and does not fall below it within 45 s after the exhaust gas recirculation valve is closed, hot exhaust gas is evidently still entering or the sensor is wrong. title: DTC P0128 - Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)

It only exists on some vehicles – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's 3.0 V6 supercharged (2013–2016, where sensor 2 is 'mid-cat' and sensor 3 'post-cat') and Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0145 means sensor 3 reacts too slowly to mixture changes, typically measured around fuel cut-off as for sensor 2 (P0139). No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – Jaguar Land Rover, the only documented user of sensor 3, does not list it. The description rests on CARB's response-rate requirement for downstream sensors and on the sensor 2 test logic. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.
symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving
possible_causes: Sensor aged or contaminated (oil ash, silicone, additives) (likelihood: high)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (likelihood: medium)
Sensor heater weak, sensor too cold (likelihood: medium)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0145 (O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 3).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: oxygen sensor bank1 sensor3, oxygen sensor wiring, catalytic converter.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.2-1 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Sensor aged or contaminated (oil ash, silicone, additives) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P0148 - Fuel Delivery Error
problem_description: P0148 is an early, rather unspecific OBD II code: the control module finds that the fuel delivered does not match what was requested. Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel (Isuzu) uses it for leak detection: from the balance of quantity and rail pressure it recognises a leak of 90 mm³ per crankshaft revolution, monitored continuously up to 6,400 rpm, and then shuts the engine off – a restart is only possible in the next drive cycle. Ford lists P0148 in the fuel monitor of its 2020–2023 petrol engines, alongside P0171/P0172, without describing the logic. Newer systems usually report such faults more precisely as P0087/P0088 (rail pressure) or P0093 (large leak).

Engine stalls or will not restart (Saab: shut-off until next drive cycle)
Loss of power, stumbling
Fuel smell with an external leak
possible_causes: Fuel leak in the high-pressure or return section (line, rail, injector leakage) (likelihood: high)
Fuel filter clogged or lift pump weak (likelihood: medium)
High-pressure or injection pump worn (likelihood: medium)
Pressure or volume control valve faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel system, high pressure fuel pump, fuel rail, fuel injectors.

title: DTC P0149 - Fuel Timing Error
problem_description: P0149 is a diesel code for a deviation of the actual from the target start of injection. On distributor pumps such as the Bosch VP44, a timing device sets the delivery start, and the pump control unit compares the actual position with the target. On the 2003 Saab 9-3 2.2 TiD (GM/Opel engine) P0149 means injection too early – too late is the manufacturer code P1149; it is monitored continuously above 600 rpm and leads to limp mode with limited fuel quantity. CARB has required injection timing monitoring for all diesels since model year 2010. On common-rail systems timing is mostly covered by injector-related codes, so P0149 is rare there.

Limp mode with power limitation
Starting problems up to no start
Smoke, knocking, rough running

title: DTC P014A - O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 2 Sensor 2
problem_description: The downstream oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) is used for fine mixture trim and to monitor the converter. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late, or does not reach the target level at all, after the mixture has changed. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, usually tested during deceleration fuel cut-off. Bank 2 only exists on V and boxer engines. GM checks whether the signal falls below 450 mV before about 45 g of air have passed after the forced change; failing needs two trips. Ford uses the same stuck-in-range test for bank 2, failing after three bad results in a row. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors).

Usually no noticeable change in driving
Catalyst monitor may stay incomplete (inspection readiness missing)
With a converter cause, P0420/P0430 may follow

title: DTC P0150 - O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 1
problem_description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0150 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0130. Ford used it up to 2010 as the collective code for wiring faults of the bank 2 wide-band sensor reported by the interface chip and has used specific codes since 2011 (P0151, P0152, P2240/P2247/P2254). Other makers fill it as for bank 1 – an interface voltage check, a collective code or a plausibility test. No bank 2-specific manufacturer thresholds were found. If P0130 and P0150 appear together, look for a shared cause such as supply, ground or the control module. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

title: DTC P015E - Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Fuel Timing Control
problem_description: Diesel fuel systems correct injection timing and quantity in closed loop, often with learning routines that run during suitable overrun phases. CARB requires a fault when such feedback control does not start within a manufacturer-defined time. P015E is the code of this kind for injection timing control: the closed-loop correction does not become active in time, or does not learn. It belongs to a family of similar codes – Ford's 2023 diesels, for example, set the sister code P016D when rail pressure adaptation has learned nothing after 300 s. No manufacturer document describing P015E itself, or its threshold, was found; the description rests on CARB and the sister code. Frequent causes are learning conditions that occur too rarely, software, or injectors outside tolerance.

title: DTC P0168 - Fuel Temperature Too High
problem_description: P0168 is not a sensor fault but an operating condition, almost only on diesels: the fuel temperature sensor reports fuel hotter than a protective limit. On Saab's Bosch EDC16 diesels the code means an engine protection function is active and injection quantity is reduced. No manufacturer threshold was found, and GM's and Ford's diesel summaries do not use P0168. Whether the warning light comes on depends on the manufacturer.

title: DTC P016A - Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control

Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. Bentley and other VW group petrol engines set it together with oxygen sensor heater codes when the heater fuse holder was damaged; Ram's 3.0 EcoDiesel listed it in bulletins fixed with new software and sensors. title: DTC P016D - Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control
problem_description: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. P016D means the pressure control has not settled into closed loop, or has not learned, in the time allowed. Ford reports adaptation at its limit separately as P228E/P228F. Use on petrol engines was not found. Often there are no noticeable symptoms.

title: DTC P0176 - Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit

GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. title: DTC P018F - Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Frequent Activation
problem_description: Common-rail diesels have a pressure relief valve in the rail – usually a spring-loaded valve, on some truck engines electronically controlled. It opens on overpressure and then holds a low limp-home pressure; every opening wears the seat, and after many openings it may no longer close tightly. P018F means the valve has opened too often: the control module recognises openings from the rail pressure trace (overshoot, then a steep drop to the limp-home level) and counts them. The code therefore usually points to an underlying problem – the pressure control repeatedly lets overpressure build up. No manufacturer document describing P018F was found; the function and counting logic come from patents on large engines (example: opening at about 1950 bar, then about 800 bar).

Starting problems once the valve no longer seals
Smoke or harsh combustion noise beforehand

title: DTC P019E - Alternative Fuel Tank A Pressure Sensor Circuit
problem_description: These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. CNG is stored at up to about 250 bar (3600 psi); a regulator reduces it to a few bar for the gas rail and injectors. The tank pressure sensor A sits at or in the regulator; together with the tank temperature it gives the gas level, and it decides whether gas operation is possible. P019E is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. Ford's earlier bi-fuel CNG system showed the gauge as empty on a tank pressure sensor fault. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found; GM's bulletins only state that faults are reported like on petrol models. The description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.

problem_description: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. Tank level sensor A only exists where there is a real sender – typically LPG tanks with a float whose position is transmitted magnetically through the tank wall (Roush propane systems: 0.1–4.9 V). With CNG the 'level' is a calculated value. The documented systems report level faults under the petrol fuel level codes (Roush propane P0460–P0463, GM CNG van P0463), so no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found. P01B3 covers brief dropouts or jumps in the level signal – typically a loose contact or chafed wiring.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Gas level display wrong, jumping or empty
Range or refuelling information unreliable
possible_causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the connector (likelihood: high)
Harness chafed along the gas line or underbody (likelihood: medium)
Sensor unstable internally (likelihood: medium)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: alternative fuel tank level sensor, sensor wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Loose contact or corrosion at the connector (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P01B9 - Engine Oil Temperature Sensor B Circuit
problem_description: The engine oil temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. Sensor B is a second oil temperature sensor whose position is defined by the manufacturer. P01B9 is the general circuit fault of sensor B, the counterpart of P0195. No manufacturer document using the B-sensor codes was found, so it is unclear who fits a sensor B; the description follows sensor A and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement.

title: DTC P01CB - Cylinder 1 Injection Timing Performance - Over Retarded
problem_description: Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor. From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 1 needs clearly more energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too late – GM sets it above 80 µs of extra time, after two trips. Documented users are GM's 6.6 litre Duramax (LML, L5P) and FCA's 3.0 litre EcoDiesel; Ford reports the same function under P2B11ff. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps.

Rough idle

title: DTC P01E8 - Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open
problem_description: Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports an open control circuit – the module detects missing continuity, typically with the driver switched off. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

problem_description: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater A through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. title: DTC P0201 - Cylinder 1 Injector A Circuit/Open
problem_description: P0201 reports an electrical fault, mainly an open circuit, in the injector circuit of cylinder 1. The engine module watches each injector output: GM flags an open circuit at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more – on direct injection and diesel engines in 10 of 20 or 5 of 10 samples and with the warning light in the first trip, on some port-injected engines only after two trips. Ford's port injection reads a fault bit from the driver chip that covers open, short to ground and short to voltage alike; Ford diesels report only the open circuit here and shorts as P0261/P0262. On direct injection the affected injector is switched off; the cylinder misfires.

title: DTC P020A - Cylinder 1 Injection Timing
problem_description: P020A reports a fault in the injection timing of cylinder 1 on a diesel engine. Unlike P01CB/P01CC ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. GM uses it as an electrical check on a four-cylinder diesel and on the 6.6 litre L5P Duramax V8: at every injection the engine module measures how long the injector current takes to reach its pull-in level of 13 A. title: DTC P0213 - Cold Start Injector 1
problem_description: A cold start injector is an additional injector in the intake manifold that sprays extra fuel for a few seconds while a cold engine is cranked. In classic Bosch systems a thermo-time switch on the block powers it directly, without the engine module – such systems cannot set a code at all. A code is only possible where the engine module drives the valve and monitors its circuit, as CARB requires for output components. From the 1990s the main injectors took over cold-start enrichment, so the code only fits early OBD II engines. P0213 concerns cold start injector 1. No manufacturer using it was found in GM, Ford or Saab documents.

title: DTC P0214 - Cold Start Injector 2
problem_description: A cold start injector is an additional injector in the intake manifold that sprays extra fuel for a few seconds while a cold engine is cranked. In classic Bosch systems a thermo-time switch on the block powers it directly, without the engine module – such systems cannot set a code at all. A code is only possible where the engine module drives the valve and monitors its circuit, as CARB requires for output components. From the 1990s the main injectors took over cold-start enrichment, so the code only fits early OBD II engines. P0214 concerns cold start injector 2, for example on a second intake bank. No manufacturer using it was found in GM, Ford or Saab documents.

title: DTC P0215 - Engine Shutoff Solenoid
problem_description: The engine shutoff solenoid is the electric stop valve on older diesel injection pumps, mainly distributor pumps. It is energised with the ignition on and lets fuel into the pump; with no current a spring closes it, the pump runs dry and the engine stops – also as a safety backup if the governor fails. P0215 reports a fault in this solenoid or its supply, typically a broken coil, a sticking plunger, a blown fuse or relay, or a wiring fault. The result is either an engine that will not start or dies, or one that keeps running after switch-off. Newer diesels stop through the injectors or a fuel shutoff valve with its own codes P0005–P0007. No manufacturer document describing P0215 was found; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components and a Bosch patent on the valve.

title: DTC P0216 - Injector/Injection Timing Control Circuit
problem_description: P0216 is a diesel code for the control of injection timing. On 1990s distributor pumps with an electronic timing advance it meant that actual injection timing missed its target; today manufacturers use it for the electronic injector control, with different meanings. GM's Duramax diesels compare, inside the engine module, the summed injection pulse widths from the hardware driver with those calculated by the software; a mismatch in 30 of 124 or 60 consecutive checks sets the code with the warning light in the first trip. On GM's 3.0 litre LM2 it appeared together with P0202 from a broken pin in the injector 2 connector. Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel uses it for a fault in the separate injector power stage. The result can be loss of power, rough running, smoke and limp mode.

title: DTC P0217 - Engine Coolant Over Temperature Condition
problem_description: P0217 is a condition code: the engine module reports that coolant temperature has passed a protection threshold. The limit and the reaction depend on the manufacturer – Saab's 2.2 diesel sets it at 120 °C for over 10 s, limits fuel quantity and suspends EGR and boost diagnostics until the temperature drops; heavy-duty diesels cut power sharply and may shut down; Ford petrol engines use their own code P1299 and cut fuel to individual cylinders. Whether the warning light comes on varies, because CARB exempts overheat protection that only engages once the gauge reads red. Usual causes are low coolant, a thermostat stuck closed, a failed fan or water pump – but Ford traced some cases to a faulty coolant sensor or harness.

title: DTC P0219 - Engine Overspeed Condition
problem_description: P0219 is a condition code: engine speed has exceeded the overspeed limit even though the rev limiter already cuts fuel – so the engine was driven from outside, usually by downshifting at too high a road speed or descending in too low a gear, or the speed signal was wrong. title: DTC P021A - Cylinder 7 Injection Timing
problem_description: P021A reports a fault in the injection timing of cylinder 7 on a diesel engine. Unlike P01D7/P01D8 ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. GM uses it as an electrical check on the 6.6 litre L5P Duramax V8: at every injection the engine module measures how long the injector current takes to reach its pull-in level of 13 A. If on the V8 that time is outside 60–150 µs in 10 of 20 samples, the code sets and the warning light comes on in the first trip. For 2020–2021 Silverado/Sierra HD, GM issued a software update against false setting. FCA's V6 and Ford do not use it.

title: DTC P0220 - Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch B Circuit
problem_description: With electronic throttle control the throttle body carries two position sensors, A and B, usually with opposite or offset signals, and the engine module compares them (correlation code P2135). GM and Ford give the pedal sensors their own codes (P2120 ff), so B is in practice the second throttle sensor. P0220 is the general circuit fault of sensor B without telling low from high. Newer GM and Ford engines report sensor B faults as P0222/P0223. The module carries on with sensor A, limits throttle opening and power and switches off cruise control.

title: DTC P022A - Charge Air Cooler Bypass Control A Circuit/Open
problem_description: The charge air cooler bypass is a flap or valve that routes compressed air around the charge air cooler, so the engine and exhaust warm up faster after a cold start; when warm it closes or opens partly to control intake air temperature. title: DTC P0230 - Fuel Pump Primary Circuit
problem_description: The fuel pump circuit has two sides: the primary circuit is the engine module's output to the fuel pump relay coil (or to a pump control module), the secondary circuit is the power circuit from relay contact or module to the pump itself. P0230 concerns the primary side. GM's output driver compares the commanded with the actual state of the relay control circuit and sets the code at 8 of 10 mismatches, after two trips; Ford checks for open or short circuits for 2–5 s. With a failed relay control the pump stays off and the engine will not start or dies; a short to voltage keeps the pump running and drains the battery. On Ford systems with a pump control module the code means its power relay circuit; on the Subaru-based Saab 9-2X it is the pump module's collective fault report.

Engine stalls while driving
Check engine light on
No pump prime noise at ignition on; with a short to voltage the pump runs on and drains the battery

Control wire from module to relay open or shorted to ground or voltage (likelihood: medium)
Relay supply, ground or fuse missing (likelihood: medium)
With a pump control module: its supply, ground or the module itself (likelihood: medium)
Engine module driver faulty (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0234 - Turbocharger/Supercharger A Overboost Condition

title: DTC P024E - Charge Air Cooler Bypass Position Sensor A Circuit Low
problem_description: The charge air cooler bypass is a flap or valve that routes compressed air around the charge air cooler, so the engine and exhaust warm up faster after a cold start; when warm it closes or opens partly to control intake air temperature. title: DTC P0263 - Cylinder 1 Contribution/Balance
problem_description: P0263 comes from the cylinder balance control of common-rail diesels: the engine module measures the crankshaft acceleration of each cylinder's power stroke, compares it with the average and gives a deviating cylinder more or less fuel. The code sets when the correction for cylinder 1 reaches its limit and the cylinder still does not keep up – GM at 95 % of a limit of about ±12–17 mm³ for 30 s, Ford above 90 % of the allowed 3.5–15 mg per stroke for 7.5 s; GM needs two trips. The code does not say whether there is too much or too little fuel – the correction value for cylinder 1 shows the direction: strongly negative means a leaking injector, strongly positive a weak injector or low compression. VW and Ram traced some cases to over-sensitive software, so check for updates before replacing injectors.

Rough idle, shaking or knocking
Loss of power or smoke
Higher consumption, poor cold start

Engine software outdated or diagnosis too sensitive (likelihood: medium)
Injector correction codes not or wrongly programmed after replacement (likelihood: medium)
Low compression on cylinder 1 (valve, rings, injector seal) (likelihood: medium)
Crankshaft sensor or tone wheel learning faulty, dual-mass flywheel (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P026B - Injection Timing Performance
problem_description: P026B is the engine-wide injection timing monitor: CARB requires diesels from 2010 to detect injection that is too early or too late overall, or a timing control at its limit. title: DTC P026F - Coolant Thermostat Performance
problem_description: P026F is a general functional code for the coolant thermostat. CARB requires that the coolant reaches the temperature needed for other diagnostics in the approved time and comes within 11 °C of the thermostat's regulating temperature; from model years 2019–2021 petrol engines must also detect it dropping back below that temperature, and electric pumps or valves controlling coolant flow are monitored like a thermostat. The module follows coolant temperature against a heat model. No manufacturer using P026F was found – GM and Ford report thermostat faults as P0128, P01F0 or P2181 – so the description rests on CARB and the thermostat's function.

title: DTC P0272 - Cylinder 4 Contribution/Balance
problem_description: P0272 comes from the cylinder balance control of common-rail diesels: the engine module measures the crankshaft acceleration of each cylinder's power stroke, compares it with the average and gives a deviating cylinder more or less fuel. The code sets when the correction for cylinder 4 reaches its limit and the cylinder still does not keep up – GM at 95 % of a limit of about ±12–17 mm³ for 30 s, Ford above 90 % of the allowed 3.5–15 mg per stroke for 7.5 s; GM needs two trips. The code does not say whether there is too much or too little fuel – the correction value for cylinder 4 shows the direction: strongly negative means a leaking injector, strongly positive a weak injector or low compression. VW and Ram traced some cases to over-sensitive software, so check for updates before replacing injectors.

Rough idle, shaking or knocking
Loss of power or smoke
Higher consumption, poor cold start

Injector correction codes not or wrongly programmed after replacement (likelihood: medium)
Low compression on cylinder 4 (valve, rings, injector seal) (likelihood: medium)
Crankshaft sensor or tone wheel learning faulty, dual-mass flywheel (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0281 - Cylinder 7 Contribution/Balance
problem_description: P0281 comes from the cylinder balance control of common-rail diesels: the engine module measures the crankshaft acceleration of each cylinder's power stroke, compares it with the average and gives a deviating cylinder more or less fuel. The code sets when the correction for cylinder 7 reaches its limit and the cylinder still does not keep up – GM at 95 % of a limit of about ±12–17 mm³ for 30 s, Ford above 90 % of the allowed 3.5–15 mg per stroke for 7.5 s; GM needs two trips. The code does not say whether there is too much or too little fuel – the correction value for cylinder 7 shows the direction: strongly negative means a leaking injector, strongly positive a weak injector or low compression.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Rough idle, shaking or knocking
Loss of power or smoke
Higher consumption, poor cold start
possible_causes: Injector of cylinder 7 worn, coked or leaking (likelihood: high)
Engine software outdated or diagnosis too sensitive (likelihood: medium)
Injector correction codes not or wrongly programmed after replacement (likelihood: medium)
Low compression on cylinder 7 (valve, rings, injector seal) (likelihood: medium)
Crankshaft sensor or tone wheel learning faulty, dual-mass flywheel (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0281 (Cylinder 7 Contribution/Balance).

problem_description: P0288 means the control wire of the cylinder 10 injector – the side the engine module switches to ground – is shorted to ground. GM detects this with the driver off: on direct injection at 1 V or less, on port injection and Duramax diesels at 0.5 Ω or less to ground. Ford's 6.7 diesel has its driver chip report the short within 0.3 s. Most systems switch the warning light on in the first trip (some GM port-injection engines and Saab's 2.0 turbo after two) and shut the affected injector off, so the cylinder misfires. Ford petrol engines report all injector circuit faults as P0201 ff instead. Cylinder 10 exists only on ten-cylinder engines; no manufacturer document using this code was found – Ford's V10 uses P0201–P0210 and GM has no V10 – so the description follows CARB and the codes for cylinders 1–8.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Misfire and rough running, misfire code P0310
Loss of power, rough idle
Injector shut off, limp mode possible on diesels
possible_causes: Control wire of the cylinder 10 injector chafed to ground in the harness (likelihood: high)
Injector connector damp or corroded, leakage to ground (likelihood: medium)
Injector shorted to its housing internally (likelihood: medium)
Open control wire (on some GM port-injection drivers this also reads low; P020x sets too) (likelihood: low)
Driver stage in the engine module faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel injector cylinder 10, injector wiring, engine control module.

Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Control wire of the cylinder 10 injector chafed to ground in the harness (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P0290 - Cylinder 10 Contribution/Balance
problem_description: P0290 comes from the cylinder balance control of common-rail diesels: the engine module measures the crankshaft acceleration of each cylinder's power stroke, compares it with the average and gives a deviating cylinder more or less fuel. The code sets when the correction for cylinder 10 reaches its limit and the cylinder still does not keep up – GM at 95 % of a limit of about ±12–17 mm³ for 30 s, Ford above 90 % of the allowed 3.5–15 mg per stroke for 7.5 s; GM needs two trips. The code does not say whether there is too much or too little fuel – the correction value for cylinder 10 shows the direction: strongly negative means a leaking injector, strongly positive a weak injector or low compression. Cylinder 10 only exists on diesels with ten cylinders; GM and Ford documents stop at cylinder 8, so the description follows CARB and the siblings.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Rough idle, shaking or knocking
Loss of power or smoke
Higher consumption, poor cold start
possible_causes: Injector of cylinder 10 worn, coked or leaking (likelihood: high)
Engine software outdated or diagnosis too sensitive (likelihood: medium)
Injector correction codes not or wrongly programmed after replacement (likelihood: medium)
Low compression on cylinder 10 (valve, rings, injector seal) (likelihood: medium)
Crankshaft sensor or tone wheel learning faulty, dual-mass flywheel (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0290 (Cylinder 10 Contribution/Balance).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel injector cylinder 10, crankshaft position sensor, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours

The code sets when the correction for cylinder 12 reaches its limit and the cylinder still does not keep up – GM at 95 % of a limit of about ±12–17 mm³ for 30 s, Ford above 90 % of the allowed 3.5–15 mg per stroke for 7.5 s; GM needs two trips. The code does not say whether there is too much or too little fuel – the correction value for cylinder 12 shows the direction: strongly negative means a leaking injector, strongly positive a weak injector or low compression. Cylinder 12 only exists on diesels with twelve cylinders; GM and Ford documents stop at cylinder 8, so the description follows CARB and the siblings.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Rough idle, shaking or knocking
Loss of power or smoke
Higher consumption, poor cold start
possible_causes: Injector of cylinder 12 worn, coked or leaking (likelihood: high)
Engine software outdated or diagnosis too sensitive (likelihood: medium)
Injector correction codes not or wrongly programmed after replacement (likelihood: medium)
Low compression on cylinder 12 (valve, rings, injector seal) (likelihood: medium)
Crankshaft sensor or tone wheel learning faulty, dual-mass flywheel (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0296 (Cylinder 12 Contribution/Balance).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel injector cylinder 12, crankshaft position sensor, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Injector of cylinder 12 worn, coked or leaking (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Engine software outdated or diagnosis too sensitive (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P0297 - Vehicle Overspeed Condition
problem_description: P0297 is a condition code: the engine module detects that road speed – from the vehicle speed sensor or wheel and output shaft speed – exceeded the calibrated maximum. Electronic speed limiters cut fuel or throttle at that limit, and the event is stored. Ford uses the code on its petrol trucks and stores it without the warning light; no manufacturer publishes a threshold. Common triggers are descending with a trailer beyond the limiter speed, wheelspin on the driven axle, a wrongly programmed tyre size or axle ratio, or spikes in the speed signal. Unlike P0219 it concerns road speed, not engine speed.
symptoms: Usually no warning light, code only stored
Vehicle limits speed at its maximum
With a disturbed signal: jumping speedometer, odd shifting
possible_causes: Limiter speed genuinely exceeded (downhill, trailer) (likelihood: high)
Wrong tyre size or axle ratio programmed, larger wheels fitted (likelihood: medium)
Wheelspin on the driven axle (likelihood: medium)
Speed signal disturbed (loose contact, interference, tone wheel) (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0297 (Vehicle Overspeed Condition).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: vehicle speed sensor, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.2-1 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Limiter speed genuinely exceeded (downhill, trailer) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Wrong tyre size or axle ratio programmed, larger wheels fitted (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P0298 - Engine Oil Over Temperature
problem_description: P0298 is a protection code: engine oil temperature – from its own sensor, often combined with the oil level sensor, or modelled – has exceeded the protection limit. Saab's 3.0 diesel limits injection quantity when the oil stays at 135 °C or more for over 10 s, until it cools down; a heavy-duty bus engine warns in two stages and then derates. Ford stores the code without the warning light, in line with CARB's exemption for overheat protection. Usual causes are high load in heat, cooling problems, a clogged oil cooler or stuck oil thermostat, and occasionally a sensor reading too high.
symptoms: Reduced power, quantity limited
Oil temperature warning
Usually no check engine light
possible_causes: High load in heat (trailer, mountain pass, stop-and-go) (likelihood: high)
Cooling or fan problem (clogged radiator, fan, thermostat, low coolant) (likelihood: medium)
Oil cooler clogged or oil thermostat stuck (likelihood: medium)
Oil temperature or level sensor reading too high (likelihood: medium)
Low oil level or wrong oil (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: engine oil temperature sensor, oil cooler, cooling system.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.

title: DTC P0299 - Turbocharger/Supercharger A Underboost Condition
problem_description: P0299 means actual boost stays below target for a period although the control already demands more. Thresholds: GM petrol 30–55 kPa below target with the warning light in the first trip; GM diesels 10–50 kPa, two trips; Ford EcoBoost more than 4 psi (about 28 kPa) for 5 s with the wastegate already commanded fully closed; Ford diesels 30–40 kPa for 10–15 s, with a further underboost code P2263. Typical causes from manufacturer bulletins: a charge air leak, a wastegate that lost its preload or whose rod came off, a leaking bypass valve, sticking turbo vanes on diesels, and ice in the charge air cooler in winter. A faulty boost sensor can also fake underboost. Many engines then limit power.
symptoms: Loss of power, sluggish acceleration
Limp mode, power limited
Check engine light on
Whistling or hissing from the charge air path under load
possible_causes: Leak in the charge air path (hose off or torn, cooler leaking, clamps) (likelihood: high)
Wastegate faulty (rod off, preload lost, vacuum or solenoid, diaphragm) (likelihood: high)
Turbo vanes sticking or turbo worn (diesel) (likelihood: medium)
Bypass valve leaking (torn diaphragm) or its control (likelihood: medium)
Ice in the charge air cooler, boost sensor or connector, or software (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0299 (Turbocharger/Supercharger A Underboost Condition).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger, wastegate, charge air hoses, boost pressure sensor a.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-6 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Leak in the charge air path (hose off or torn, cooler leaking, clamps) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Wastegate faulty (rod off, preload lost, vacuum or solenoid, diaphragm) (likelihood: high).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
