title: DTC P029A - Cylinder 1 - Fuel Trim at Max Limit
problem_description: These codes belong to an individual-cylinder fuel correction: a diesel's cylinder balance control measures each cylinder's crankshaft acceleration and adjusts its injection quantity; on petrol engines a cylinder-selective mixture control does the same. CARB requires the system to report when such a correction has used up its range or one cylinder causes an imbalance. P029A means the correction for cylinder 1 is at its upper limit: the module keeps giving this cylinder more fuel and still cannot even it out – a sign that the cylinder receives too little fuel or builds too little pressure. GM and Ford use other codes for this (P0263 ff, P219A ff); no manufacturer document describing this code with thresholds was found, so the description follows CARB and published patents.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Rough idle, vibration
Lack of power, possibly misfire
possible_causes: Injector of cylinder 1 coked or partly clogged (likelihood: high)
Compression loss in this cylinder (valve, rings, leak at injector or glow plug) (likelihood: medium)
Injector circuit high-resistance or connector (likelihood: medium)
Petrol: false air at this cylinder's intake (manifold gasket) (likelihood: medium)
Injector correction code missing or wrong after replacement (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P029A (Cylinder 1 - Fuel Trim at Max Limit).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel injector cylinder 1, crankshaft position sensor, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-4 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Injector of cylinder 1 coked or partly clogged (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Compression loss in this cylinder (valve, rings, leak at injector or glow plug) (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

title: DTC P02CC - Cylinder 1 Fuel Injector A Offset Learning At Min Limit
problem_description: The engine module learns a small-quantity correction for each injector: on overrun it gives one injector a tiny test injection (GM about 1.5 mm³), measures the resulting crankshaft acceleration and corrects the injector's activation time per rail pressure step. P02CC means the learned correction for cylinder 1 has reached its lower limit at at least one pressure step: the injector needs much less activation time than nominal – it delivers too much at small quantities or opens early. GM diesels set it at limits of roughly ±66–182 µs after two trips. It is documented on GM's 6.6 litre L5P and 2.8 litre diesels – on the 2.8 a worn drive belt caused it to return after injector replacement – and on Land Rover's 5.0 V8 petrol, where a software update is the first step. It differs from P01CC (over advanced), which some systems derive from the same learning.

problem_description: Cold start fuel injection is an extra injection system for cold starts – for example on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends, where a Hyundai patent describes a small auxiliary tank, a cold-start injector and a heater. CARB lists such heated fuel preparation systems among the monitored output components. P02FB means the control circuit of the cold-start injection is open or has a general fault – a broken coil, a loose or corroded connector or a broken wire. The engine then starts poorly or not at all in the cold; once warm it runs normally. No manufacturer document using this code was found; unlike the older P0213/P0214, these codes separate the fault types.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Hard or no start in cold weather (especially with high ethanol)
Rough running right after a cold start
possible_causes: Coil of the cold-start injector or valve open (likelihood: high)
Connector loose, corroded or pin pushed back (likelihood: medium)
Broken wire in the harness (likelihood: medium)
Fuse or relay of the cold-start system (likelihood: low)
Driver stage in the engine module (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P02FB (Cold Start Fuel Injection Control Circuit/Open).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: cold start injector, cold start fuel system, injector wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Coil of the cold-start injector or valve open (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Connector loose, corroded or pin pushed back (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P02FF - Propulsion System Inactive Timer Performance
problem_description: Many diagnostics need to know how long the engine – or, on hybrids, the whole propulsion system – has been off: thermostat and evaporative checks and the cold-start strategy, for which CARB requires at least 6 hours of standstill. A timer measures this time, and the engine module checks its plausibility, for example against coolant cooling – a GM patent describes such a check. P02FF means that timer is implausible. Mercedes documents it on M256, M260, M264 and M274 engines of around 2020: after an internal reset the instrument cluster clock ran wrong; the fix is a software update for engine, transmission and instrument cluster modules. Readiness of standstill-dependent monitors may stay incomplete.
symptoms: Check engine light on, otherwise usually nothing noticeable
Clock in the instrument cluster wrong or reset
Readiness of standstill-dependent monitors incomplete
possible_causes: Time source in another module (instrument cluster, body module) gives an implausible time after a reset or voltage loss (likelihood: high)
Software level of engine, transmission or instrument cluster module (likelihood: high)
Battery discharged or disconnected, voltage dips (likelihood: medium)
Instrument cluster or timer in the engine module faulty (likelihood: low)
Coolant temperature sensor distorting the cooling check (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P02FF (Propulsion System Inactive Timer Performance).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: engine control module, instrument cluster, engine off timer.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.3-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Time source in another module (instrument cluster, body module) gives an implausible time after a reset or voltage loss (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Software level of engine, transmission or instrument cluster module (likelihood: high).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

title: DTC P0300 - Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected
problem_description: The engine module detects misfire from crankshaft speed: a cylinder that does not fire gives no acceleration impulse. At a catalyst-damaging rate (CARB: at least 5 % per 200 revolutions) the warning light flashes; at an emissions-relevant rate (at least 1 % per 1,000 revolutions – GM about 2–5 %, Ford 0.9–1.5 %) it comes on after two trips. Ford and GM may shut off a misfiring cylinder's injector to protect the catalyst. P0300 sets when the misfire cannot be assigned to one cylinder: several cylinders each account for more than 10 %, the cylinder changes randomly, or – at Ford – the cylinder cannot be identified at high speed. It often appears together with cylinder codes. Causes are usually systemic: false air, worn plugs on several cylinders, fuel pressure or fuel quality, valve timing – and false detection from a damaged tone wheel, rough roads or vibration. Bulletins name coils, cracked plug insulators and wrong plug gaps.
symptoms: Check engine light on, flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate
Rough idle, jerking, vibration
Loss of power, hesitation
Smell of unburnt fuel, higher consumption
possible_causes: False air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket) (likelihood: high)
Worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils (likelihood: high)
Fuel pressure too low or high, contaminated fuel (likelihood: medium)
Valve timing (stretched chain), valves, compression on several cylinders (likelihood: low)
False detection: tone wheel or pulley, rough road, vibration, software (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0300 (Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: ignition system, fuel system, intake system, crankshaft position sensor.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-6 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: False air (vacuum leak, crankcase ventilation, intake gasket) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Worn or wrong spark plugs on several cylinders, faulty ignition coils (likelihood: high).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P0315 - Crankshaft Position System Variation Not Learned
problem_description: Manufacturing tolerances of the crankshaft tone wheel distort the speed fluctuations misfire detection relies on, so the engine module learns a correction for each tooth or segment. P0315 means these values have not been learned or are invalid. GM checks that the learned tooth angles add up to 360° (deviation above 0.001° sets the code in the first trip) and learns them with a scan tool: brakes held, full throttle in park until fuel cut-off. Ford learns the profile during up to three overrun phases from 60 to 40 mph and sets P0315 when that fails. Until relearned, misfire detection is suspended – at GM above 1,000 rpm – and misfire readiness stays incomplete. The relearn is needed after replacing the engine, engine module, crankshaft, damper or crankshaft sensor.

title: DTC P0316 - Engine Misfire Detected on Startup (First 1000 Revolutions)
problem_description: P0316 concerns misfire within the first 1,000 revolutions after start. title: DTC P031A - Ignition C Control Signal Circuit/Open
problem_description: Ignition C is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. problem_description: P0320 originally covered the engine speed signal from the distributor or ignition module to the engine module (early OBD II); today Ford's engine module evaluates the crankshaft sensor directly and uses this code for it. title: DTC P0322 - Ignition/Distributor Engine Speed Input Circuit No Signal
problem_description: P0322 means the speed and reference input of the ignition – today the crankshaft position sensor – delivers no signal although the engine is turning. title: DTC P032F - Combustion Engine Producing Insufficient Torque
problem_description: P032F is a plausibility code: the engine module compares the torque the combustion engine actually delivers with the expected or requested torque. On hybrids the actual torque can be measured precisely through the generator; if it stays too low for a calibrated time, the code sets. Stellantis lists it on the Ram 6.7 Cummins for engine stall detection. Thresholds are not published.

title: DTC P033F - Crankshaft/Camshaft Loss Of Synchronization
problem_description: To know which stroke each cylinder is in, the engine module matches the crank angle with the camshaft phase. title: DTC P034A - Crankshaft Position Sensor - Crankshaft Start Position Incorrect
problem_description: Engines with start-stop or hybrid autostart store the crankshaft rest position when the engine stops, so that they can inject and fire correctly at once on restart. This needs a direction-sensing crank sensor, because a cylinder under compression can push the crankshaft backwards after shut-off. The check is suspended while a crank sensor fault is present. Result: start-stop is restricted, restarts take longer with conventional synchronisation, and the autostart may be rough.

title: DTC P0363 - Misfire Detected - Fueling Disabled
problem_description: P0363 is a reaction code: the engine module has detected misfire severe enough to damage the catalyst – through its crankshaft-based misfire monitor – and has therefore shut off injection to the affected cylinder or cylinders. CARB allows exactly this: a vehicle that cuts fuel immediately on catalyst-damaging misfire may turn the check engine light on steadily instead of flashing it, and may switch fuel back on to re-check at most every 30 s. The code names no cylinder; that comes from the accompanying P0301 ff. It is documented by code only at FCA: two reprogramming bulletins for the 2017–2018 Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 turbo list P0363 alongside misfire and mixture codes. Ford reacts in the same way without its own code, VW uses a manufacturer code (P130A) for the hidden cylinder, and GM does not list P0363.

title: DTC P0365 - Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
problem_description: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0365 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM sets it after 4 s of cranking or 5.5 s without a cam pulse, or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, 8 of 10 samples, after two trips; on GM's 3.6-litre V6 (Saab 9-4X) also with no pulse in 800 of 1,000 engine cycles. Ford checks the ratio of crank to cam events from 200 rpm, detected within 5 s, and collects all electrical faults here. The exhaust phaser then goes to its park position; the engine keeps running but cranks longer and loses some power. FCA advises saving the cam/crank synchronisation data before replacing the sensor, as the fault is often elsewhere.

title: DTC P036A - Ignition G Control Signal Circuit/Open

title: DTC P0370 - Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A
problem_description: Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal, to time and meter injection precisely – the high resolution signal. title: DTC P037C - Cold Start Camshaft Profile System Performance
problem_description: To heat the catalyst quickly after a cold start, some engines select a particular camshaft profile; CARB counts altered valve timing among these cold-start measures and requires components of the cold-start strategy to have their own diagnostics. Two GM bulletins (19-NA-145 for 2019 Silverado/Sierra 1500 with stalling on remote start below −6 °C, 20-NA-174 for the 2020 Cadillac CT4) trace P037C to a software fault and reprogram the engine module.

title: DTC P037D - Glow Plug Sense Circuit

problem_description: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0390 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive from bank 2 while the crankshaft turns. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) sets it after 5.5 s without a cam pulse, 4 s of cranking or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s, after two trips; for GM it collects all circuit faults. The bank 2 exhaust phaser then locks in its base position; the engine keeps running on the crank and intake cam sensors. FCA advises saving the synchronisation data before replacing the sensor.

title: DTC P03D6 - Cylinder 7 Pressure Too Low

title: DTC P03E9 - A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Exceeded Learning Limit
problem_description: Engines with cam profile switching move the intake camshaft between lift profiles with actuators – for example pins that shift a sliding cam – and position sensors report which profile is engaged. The engine module learns reference values of position sensor A, such as its end-position levels or the expected pulse position relative to the crankshaft and camshaft sensors; a Ford patent describes correcting this position for the cam phase. P03E9 means the learned value lies outside the permitted adaptation limit, so profile detection is no longer reliable and the module usually stays in a safe profile. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code or its limits; GM's 2.7-litre sliding cam has no learning-limit code. CARB lists a pin that does not reach its position among the faults to be detected.

Actuator C is the third of these actuators – not a profile position. The only known user is GM's 2.7-litre turbo four (L3B, three-step sliding cam, from model year 2019). P03F0 means the actuator stays on: its pin remains extended although it was commanded off. GM checks whether the pin returns past its retraction threshold by the end of the engine cycle; a single failure in 5 samples sets the code (MIL on the first trip), because a pin left extended can drag in the groove and shift the piece wrongly.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Ticking or rattling at the camshaft carrier
Misfire, rough idle or less power in the wrong lift profile
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation out of service
possible_causes: Pin sticking in the actuator (sludge, wear) (likelihood: high)
Return ramp of the shift groove damaged or cam piece sticking (likelihood: medium)
Solenoid stays energized (control wire shorted to ground) (likelihood: medium)
Hall feedback faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P03F0 (A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Stuck On Bank 1).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: camshaft profile actuator c intake, sliding camshaft, actuator wiring, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-8 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Pin sticking in the actuator (sludge, wear) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Return ramp of the shift groove damaged or cam piece sticking (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P03F1 - B Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Circuit/Open Bank 1

title: DTC P03F6 - B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
problem_description: On some engines the exhaust cam phaser (camshaft position actuator B) has its own position sensors, which tell the engine module where the phaser actually is; sensor C is the third of them, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. This is a different family from the sliding-cam position sensors (P2C05 ff). P03F6 is the general circuit code for this sensor: the module sees an open circuit or a signal outside its valid window on the supply, signal or ground line. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code (GM, Ford and FCA tables checked); the intake counterpart P03E5 ff is equally unused. The phaser is then usually held in its base position.

title: DTC P03FA - Ignition K Control Signal Circuit/Open
problem_description: Ignition K is one of up to twelve control signal lines (A to L) from the engine module to an ignition coil with integrated output stage or to an ignition module – plausibly the 11th channel, but the code standard leaves the assignment to the manufacturer. The code concerns this logic-level signal, not the coil's primary circuit (coil K has its own codes, P0361 and P2330 ff). P03FA means the control line is open or high-resistance: with its driver switched off the module sees a voltage that indicates a missing load (GM uses more than 30 kΩ for comparable coil drivers). The coil fires wrongly or not at all; the misfire usually also sets P0300 ff, and many modules shut off injection to that cylinder to protect the catalyst. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it would only concern twelve-cylinder engines, whose makers publish no OBD summaries; GM and Ford tables stop at eight and ten cylinders.

Misfire on the cylinder of this channel, rough running
Loss of power, cylinder possibly shut off
possible_causes: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin) (likelihood: high)
Coil with integrated output stage or ignition module faulty (likelihood: medium)
Supply or ground of the coil or module missing (likelihood: medium)
Driver in the engine module (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P044A - EGR Sensor C Circuit

What EGR sensor C is depends on the maker: on Ford petrol engines from 2020 it is the DPFE sensor, which measures the pressure drop across an orifice in the EGR pipe (sensor A there is the valve position sensor); GM diesels assign it to the position sensor of a low-pressure EGR valve, but only within fault groups. P044A is the general circuit fault of this sensor. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – Ford splits it into P044C/P044D – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. Without the sensor, EGR flow and cooler checks are suspended.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
EGR readiness not set, EGR possibly switched off
possible_causes: Connector or wire to sensor C open or corroded (likelihood: high)
Sensor faulty (likelihood: medium)
5 V reference or ground disturbed (with other sensor codes) (likelihood: medium)
Engine module (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P044A (EGR Sensor C Circuit).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: egr sensor c, dpfe sensor, sensor wiring, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Connector or wire to sensor C open or corroded (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Sensor faulty (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P044F - AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit High
problem_description: After a cold start the secondary air pump blows fresh air into the exhaust; switching valve A is the electrically driven valve that opens this path. GM checks the valve circuit in three codes – P0412 open, P041F shorted to ground, P044F shorted to positive – while other makers use P0413/P0414 or P0412 for everything. P044F means the control circuit is shorted to positive or the coil is low-resistance: when the driver switches on, the line stays high. GM sets the code at 0.5 Ω or less to the supply (20 of 25 samples of 250 ms, above 11 V, MIL after two trips). The valve then does not open, secondary air is missing and P0411 may follow.

problem_description: The evaporative emission (EVAP) system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister; a purge valve lets the engine draw it off, and a vent valve opens the canister to fresh air. Purge valve A is switched to ground by the module and fed from the main relay. P0459 means its control wire is shorted to positive, detected with the driver switched on, when the line should sit at ground (GM 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips; Saab ME9 above 4.6 V). The valve then cannot open, the canister is not purged and fills up; the driver protects itself and the leak tests are suspended.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Fuel smell when the canister is full
EVAP readiness not set
possible_causes: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or supply (likelihood: high)
Purge valve coil low-resistance (shorted turns) (likelihood: medium)
Connector or harness damaged (likelihood: medium)
Engine module (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0459 (EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Circuit High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: evap purge valve, purge valve wiring, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or supply (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Purge valve coil low-resistance (shorted turns) (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P0460 - Fuel Level Sensor A Circuit

P0460 is the general circuit code for sensor A, the main or only fuel level sensor. Ford sets it instead of P0462/P0463 below 5 Ω or above 200 Ω for 30 s and until about 2012 also used it for a stuck sensor (fuel use compared over 100–120 miles); Saab's Trionic T8 uses it for a sensor that does not change. GM does not use P0460. The gauge then shows wrong values or a substitute, and level-dependent monitors do not run.

title: DTC P049A - EGR B Flow
problem_description: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Usually soot at the seat keeps the valve from closing, or a new valve was not taught in.

title: DTC P04DB - Crankcase Ventilation System Disconnected
problem_description: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04DB means a disconnection: without the pressure drop the clean-air side is off, without the pulses the crankcase side. GM's LSY uses the product of normalised offset and noise (below 0.63 kPa², MIL after two trips); Ford's EcoBoost checks the dirty side at cranking and the clean side above 5 lb/min of air. Engines without such a sensor may report a disconnection through mixture or load codes, as CARB allows. FCA bulletins cover it on the Alfa Romeo 2.0 turbo and the Ram 3.0 EcoDiesel.

title: DTC P04DC - Fuel Fill Door Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance
problem_description: Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. When the driver presses the fuel button, the system opens the valve, lets the pressure escape into the canister and only then unlocks the filler door. A switch reports whether the door is open or closed, so that the tank can be sealed again afterwards. P04DC means the door switch signal is electrically valid but implausible. A GM patent detects refuelling from a rising fuel level at standstill with low tank pressure; if the switch reported open for less than about 20 s, or closed for too long, it is faulty. A Ford patent sets a fault if the fuel level rose and the car drove off without the switch ever reporting open – the valve then stays open and the driver is warned. If the door state is unknown, the system leaves the tank open to the canister as a precaution and suspends the leak tests. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules and patents for the door switch.

title: DTC P04F2 - Catalyst Heater Supply Voltage Bank 1
problem_description: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04F2 concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code monitors the supply voltage of the heater: if it lies outside its window when heating is requested, the heater cannot deliver its power and is limited or switched off, so the catalyst lights off later. A Subaru patent detects faults in the supply path when the heater is commanded. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.
symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Higher emissions after a cold start
Otherwise usually unremarkable
possible_causes: 48 V or high-voltage supply weak (battery, charge, cold, DC-DC converter) (likelihood: high)
Fuse, relay or power switch faulty (likelihood: medium)
Contact resistance or corrosion at high-current connector or ground (likelihood: medium)
Module or voltage measurement faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P04F2 (Catalyst Heater Supply Voltage Bank 1).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: catalyst heater bank1, heater power switch, heater wiring, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

title: DTC P04FD - EGR Actuator A Control Processor Performance
problem_description: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04FD means the actuator reports an internal processor or electronics fault, or its self-test failed. CARB does not require such internal faults to be reported, so the code is a voluntary detail. Volvo and Mack trucks with turbocompound document it with false triggers fixed by engine software. The actuator then goes to its default position and EGR is off.

title: DTC P04FE - Catalyst Heater Circuit Performance Bank 1
problem_description: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04FE concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code is the function check: the circuit is electrically sound but the effect does not fit – for example the energy delivered in a time window after switch-on stays below target, which a Toyota patent evaluates as a ratio, or the catalyst temperature does not rise as modelled. Ageing of the disc raises its resistance. The pure temperature result code is P0424/P0434. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.

Otherwise usually unremarkable

Catalyst or exhaust temperature sensor implausible (likelihood: low)
Software or calibration (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0505 - Idle Control System

P0505 is the general fault of the idle control, used where the maker does not separate too low from too high or the control is at its limit. With an idle valve it is typically sticking or gummed (Saab T5: idle outside 700–1200 rpm); on electronic throttles a Ford investigation shows P0505 from deposits in the throttle body. problem_description: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050B checks the ignition part of the strategy – the retard for catalyst heating; CARB allows checking only the commanded value. Ford sets it when desired and commanded cold-start timing differ by more than 10°, for example because knock, torque or idle control take back the retard. FCA fixed P050B on the 2.0-litre turbo Wrangler of 2018–19 with software. GM has no separate monitor.

Usually no noticeable symptoms
Catalyst warms up more slowly after a cold start

Idle control takes back the retard because speed would drop (false air, dirty throttle) (likelihood: medium)
Knock control or knock sensor intervenes (likelihood: low)
Extra load or alternator at cold start (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P050F - Brake Assist Vacuum Too Low
problem_description: GM (from about model year 2017/18) monitors the brake booster with a vacuum sensor: with the pedal at rest and high intake vacuum the booster must hold its vacuum; a loss over time is filtered as a drift ratio, and above a threshold P050F sets, MIL after two trips. title: DTC P0511 - Idle Air Control Circuit
problem_description: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0511 is the general circuit fault of the idle valve – open, short to ground or to positive – without separating low and high, which CARB permits. Ford (up to about 2012, engines with an idle valve) has the output stage report it via a diagnostic status bit, continuously. Valve types are PWM solenoid or rotary valves (two wires) or stepper motors (four wires, typical of GM). Without a working valve the engine runs on a fixed bypass or the mechanical stop and may stall.

Maserati and Alfa Romeo bulletins name blow-by valves or software.

Often no change in driving

Engine module software (known false trigger) (likelihood: medium)

problem_description: The PCV heater is an electric element of a few ohms (Saab: 6–10 Ω) at the junction of the ventilation hose and the intake; it stops water in the blow-by gas from freezing and blocking the ventilation in frost. Heater permanently on
Usually no change in driving

Heating element shorted to its housing (likelihood: medium)

title: DTC P053F - Cold Start Fuel Pressure Performance Bank 1

title: DTC P054A - Cold Start B Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced Bank 1
problem_description: Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft. During catalyst heating after a cold start some engines set it to a specific position; CARB requires such commanded elements to be monitored with their own codes, separate from the normal cam codes. Ford watches the deviation with an averaged variance index for each direction; GM (Saab 9-4X V6) uses only the retard codes, above 6° for 1 s or 4 s cumulative, type B. The commonest cause is oil pressure building too slowly when cold. P054A means bank 1 was too far advanced. Mercedes (M276) traces it to slow oil pressure – 1 bar should be reached after about 3 s; Audi (Q5 3.2) and VW (Atlas 3.6 and 2.0 T) fixed it by software.
symptoms: Check engine light on, usually without noticeable symptom
Brief rattle on cold start
Rough idle while warming up
possible_causes: Oil pressure building too slowly when cold (oil level, viscosity, pick-up, pump) (likelihood: high)
Exhaust oil control valve sticking or screens clogged (likelihood: medium)
Module software (threshold too tight) (likelihood: medium)
Cam phaser defective, locking pin (likelihood: low)

CARB names cruise control as the example of an emission-neutral diagnosis – it is simply switched off – so GM lists all these codes as type C and Ford as non-MIL: no warning lamp, the engine runs normally. P0569 concerns a separate coast button (minus, lower the speed) – stuck or implausible. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. GM combines set and coast and has no coast code of its own.
symptoms: Speed cannot be lowered with cruise control
Cruise control locked out
No check engine light, engine runs normally
possible_causes: Coast (minus) button stuck or faulty (likelihood: high)
Moisture or wear in the steering wheel switch (likelihood: medium)
Contact resistance in clockspring or steering wheel connector (likelihood: medium)
Body module or cruise module (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0569 (Cruise Control Coast Signal).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: cruise control switch, clockspring, switch wiring, body control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Coast (minus) button stuck or faulty (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Moisture or wear in the steering wheel switch (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P056D - Reductant Control Module System Voltage
problem_description: Diesels with SCR may have a separate module for AdBlue/DEF dosing (pump, heaters, dosing valve) talking to the engine module over CAN. It measures its supply; outside its window no safe dosing is possible, so dosing and SCR diagnoses are suspended and NOx rises, and if it persists the SCR warnings and power limits apply. No manufacturer document available to us uses P056D – Ford's diesel reports the dosing module supply as P21CB below 8.5 V and P21CC above 19 V. CARB requires SCR modules to be monitored.

Possible countdown to start inhibit or power limit
Further SCR codes

Corrosion at module connector or ground (underbody, road salt) (likelihood: medium)
System under- or overvoltage (likelihood: medium)
Module faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: reductant control module, module power supply, module ground.

title: DTC P056E - Cold Start Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Performance
problem_description: CARB requires every element commanded by the cold-start strategy to respond measurably in the commanded direction, with its own codes separate from the general monitoring of the same part. During catalyst heating the boost control is positioned deliberately – diesels close the variable turbine for load and heat, petrol engines open the wastegate so heat reaches the catalyst. P056E means boost control A (the first or only charger) did not follow its cold-start target. Its only documented user is Stellantis: the 2025 Ram 3500 cab chassis with 6.7 L Cummins lists it among codes that can light the warning lamp, fixed by a PCM software update; customers noticed hard cold starts and raised cold idle. Ford and GM do not use it.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Hard cold start or rough warm-up
Otherwise usually unremarkable
possible_causes: Variable turbine or wastegate actuator stiff (coking, cold) (likelihood: high)
Module software or calibration (likelihood: medium)
Vacuum or boost hose leaking (likelihood: medium)
Position or boost sensor faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbocharger actuator, boost pressure sensor, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Variable turbine or wastegate actuator stiff (coking, cold) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Module software or calibration (likelihood: medium).

title: DTC P0571 - Brake Switch A Circuit
problem_description: Brake switch A is the brake light switch or its signal to the engine module. The module needs it to cancel cruise control and for brake-throttle override, stop-start, idle control and the shift interlock. As cruise control is simply switched off, CARB treats such faults as emission-neutral – usually without warning lamp. P0571 is the general fault, usually detected by plausibility: Saab's 3.0 TiD (Bosch) sets it when the car brakes three times from over 49 km/h to standstill at 1.6 m/s² or more without a switch signal; Bosch EDC16 then switches cruise control off. NHTSA found Hyundai and Kia setting P0571 with P0504 from misadjusted brake light switches. Ford and GM petrol engines use P0572/P0573 instead.

Engine or body module (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0597 - Thermostat Heater Control Circuit/Open

CARB requires the thermostat to be monitored and the heater circuit counts as an output component. title: DTC P05CC - Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Performance Bank 1

title: DTC P05E1 - A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
problem_description: The refrigerant pressure sensor (three wires, 5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) tells the engine module the A/C pressure; it uses it to switch the radiator fan, to block the compressor at too high or too low pressure and to pre-control idle load. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults and plausibility, but they need not light the lamp if they do not affect emissions. 'Intermittent/Erratic' means the signal jumps implausibly fast or briefly leaves its valid range without staying low or high long enough for those codes. Sensor A is usually the high-pressure sensor; GM and Saab report it only as P0532/P0533 (circuit low/high, at GM below 3 % or above 98 % of 5 V) and P0531, so no manufacturer document available to us uses P05E1 itself. Typically the compressor is blocked and the fan runs. GM rates sensor A faults without the lamp, the Saab 9-4X with it.
symptoms: A/C intermittently not cooling (compressor switched off)
Radiator fan runs unnecessarily or irregularly
Idle speed fluctuates when A/C engages
Warning lamp depending on the maker
possible_causes: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector (front end, splash water) (likelihood: high)
Chafed or broken wire (5 V, signal, ground) (likelihood: medium)

title: DTC P05E8 - Engine Oil Bypass Valve Control Circuit/Open

title: DTC P05EB - Cold Start SCR NOx Catalyst Inlet Temperature Too Low

title: DTC P05EC - Cold Start Injection Timing Performance

Its supply voltage is monitored separately from the pump control circuit (P208A ff); CARB requires SCR components and their outputs to be checked for circuit faults and function. P05F0 means the supply voltage is too high, or voltage is present although the supply is switched off (short to battery). GM's 6.6 L diesel monitors this as P1044 (two trips); Ford flags pump voltage above 16 V or controller voltage above 19 V. No manufacturer document available to us uses this exact code; GM and Ford monitor the same function under their own codes. Without supply the pump cannot build pressure, dosing stops and NOx rises; pressure or SCR efficiency codes may follow.
symptoms: Check engine light on
DEF/AdBlue warning, possibly countdown to no-restart
Follow-up codes for low DEF pressure or SCR efficiency
possible_causes: Pump supply shorted to battery positive in the harness (likelihood: high)
Overvoltage from the charging system or a jump start (likelihood: medium)
Moisture or corrosion causing leakage current in the connector (likelihood: medium)
Relay or driver does not switch off (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P05F0 (Reductant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: reductant pump, reductant pump supply circuit, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Pump supply shorted to battery positive in the harness (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Overvoltage from the charging system or a jump start (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P05F3 - Exhaust Aftertreatment Power Relay Control Circuit/Open

title: DTC P05F9 - Stop-Start Status Signal Circuit
problem_description: A discrete stop-start status line tells the engine module (or another module) whether stop-start is active, inhibited or has just stopped the engine. On most current cars this status travels over CAN instead, so a hard-wired line and these codes are rare; no manufacturer document available to us uses P05F9–P05FB. CARB names stop-start as its example of an 'emissions neutral' reaction: a module that simply disables stop-start when a fault appears may report it without the check engine light, which is what Ford does for its stop-start codes. P05F9 is the general circuit fault or open line. The typical reaction is that stop-start is disabled; the driver-operated stop-start switch has its own codes.

Check engine light only with some makers

title: DTC P05FC - Cold Start Fuel Pressure Performance Bank 2
problem_description: During a cold start, direct injection petrol engines usually raise rail pressure for finer atomisation with multiple injections while the catalyst heats up. P05FC monitors whether the actual rail pressure of bank 2 stays within the target window during this phase – only engines with separate rails and pressure sensors per bank (V or boxer engines with two high-pressure circuits) can set it. CARB lists fuel pressure as a cold start component that must respond measurably beyond what would happen without the strategy. No manufacturer document available to us uses P05FC; Ford checks the single-rail counterpart P053F and flags a fault when the share of cold start time inside the pressure window is 0.70 or less, and Kia replaced the engine module of the 2018 Stinger 2.0T for P053F with stumbling during warm-up. GM uses P2C1E–P2C20 instead.

title: DTC P05FD - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Temperature Too High
problem_description: Electric variable-geometry turbo actuators use a DC motor with gearing, driven by an H-bridge in the engine module or in the actuator itself. Constant high load – sooted or stiff vanes, running against a stop, an internal motor short – drives up current and temperature. GM's 2025 diesels set P05FD when the H-bridge driver exceeds 170 °C in 240 of 300 samples (about 3 s) and light the lamp in the first trip. The driver then shuts off for protection, the actuator stops or returns to its rest position, and boost control is limited – underboost or overboost and reduced power can follow. GM Europe's earlier 2.0 diesels reported the same protection under P0046. Circuit faults of the actuator are P0045–P0048, the position sensor P2563 ff.

Possibly underboost or overboost codes (P0299/P0234)

title: DTC P05FE - Active Grille Air Shutter C Performance/Stuck Off
problem_description: Active grille shutters close the air inlet when little cooling is needed, to reduce drag and speed up warm-up. P05FE is the performance check of a third shutter C – target and actual position do not match, as P059F does for shutter A and P05AE for shutter B. Only vehicles with three separately driven shutters could set it, and no manufacturer was found that uses a shutter C: GM and Ford use only A (upper) and B (lower). This description therefore follows A and B: control is suspended and the shutter stays where it is or opens; if it sticks closed, cooling air is missing under load. GM and Ford light the lamp for A and B after two trips. Ice and debris are frequent causes, and GM fixed false A/B codes in snow by software on the 2025 Equinox. Stuck on is P2C73.
symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Higher coolant temperature under load or slower warm-up
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Often no noticeable symptoms

Louvres unhooked or broken (impact) (likelihood: medium)
Shutter C actuator faulty (likelihood: medium)
Connector, wiring or supply corroded (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P05FF - Brake Pressure Sensor/Brake Pedal Position Sensor Correlation
problem_description: Stop-start decides when to stop and restart the engine from the brake: Ford stops it when the pedal switch is on and master cylinder pressure is high enough, and restarts when pressure falls below a filtered reference. P05FF means brake pressure (from the sensor in the ABS unit, sent over the network) and brake pedal position do not agree – for example pedal pressed without pressure build-up, or pressure without pedal. Ford's 2020–23 petrol vehicles check this continuously in the section 'Brake Diagnostics for Stop-Start Dependability' and set the code within 1 s, without the check engine light; stop-start is blocked so the engine is not stopped or started unexpectedly. Ford gives no threshold for the deviation. GM monitors the pedal travel sensor under P057x instead. Brake switch disagreement is P0504.

No check engine light at Ford, possibly wrench or service warning
Possible related codes P0504 or brake pressure codes

Master cylinder pressure sensor in the ABS unit faulty (likelihood: medium)
Network communication or software between ABS module and engine module (likelihood: medium)
Air in the brake system or hydraulic fault (long pedal travel without pressure) (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0600 - Serial Communication Link
problem_description: P0600 means a serial data link that the module relies on has failed. At Ford it is the internal link between the main processor and the monitoring processor ('quizzer') of the electronic throttle safety concept: if data cannot be exchanged or check bytes are invalid, the code sets within about a second (diesel: 5 s), usually with the check engine and wrench lamps and a throttle failure mode such as an RPM limit. Subaru (also sold as Saab 9-2X) uses it for the dedicated serial line between engine and transmission module. GM does not use P0600. Lost CAN messages from a named module are reported separately as U0100 and following. Before replacing anything: check battery, grounds and supply, look for a software bulletin, reprogram with a stable power supply, and replace the module only if the code returns.

title: DTC P0601 - Internal Control Module Memory Checksum Error
problem_description: The module continuously calculates a checksum over its program and calibration memory (flash) and compares it with the stored value; on newer units the flash error correction also reports bit errors it cannot repair. A mismatch means the stored software is corrupted. GM sets P0601 in the engine module after one failed pass (or five once the first pass is complete) and turns on the lamp in the first trip; in body modules after two trips. Ford reports the same check as P0605, while GM, VW and Mazda use P0601. Typical causes are an interrupted reflash and manufacturer software errors – VW (2.0 TFSI) and Mazda (MX-5 2013) fixed it by reprogramming. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.

Possibly no start or limp mode if the software is badly damaged
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

Defective flash memory in the module (likelihood: medium)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0602 - Control Module Programming Error
problem_description: P0602 reports that the module is not, or not completely, programmed for this vehicle. GM checks at power-up and then every second whether a service replacement module still carries no calibration, and sets the code in the first trip; in brake modules a missing calibration set or a sensor ID that does not match also counts. Ford uses P0602 when the checksum of the vehicle identification block (tyre size, axle ratio, VIN) is wrong. Typical triggers are a new module that was never programmed, a reflash interrupted by a voltage dip or lost connection, or wrong software. Depending on the maker the engine may not start, run with reduced power or only show the lamp; GM Europe engines show a service lamp instead of the check engine light. The fix is almost always reprogramming with a stable power supply; replace the module only if the code returns.

title: DTC P0603 - Internal Control Module Keep Alive Memory (KAM) Error
problem_description: Keep alive memory holds learned values – fuel trim, idle and shift adaptation, readiness status – while the engine is off, as long as the module has constant battery power; CARB defines it as memory that is lost when the battery or fuse is disconnected. The module stores a checksum of this memory at shutdown and compares it at the next start (Ford, GM Europe); GM calls the check 'long term memory reset', and the Ford diesel watches the supply of its engine-off timer chip (below 0.25 V). By far the most common trigger is outside the module: a disconnected, flat or replaced battery or an interrupted constant feed – Nissan bulletins name exactly this and ask for at least 11 V before clearing. Learned values then start from default and the readiness monitors are reset. Whether the lamp comes on depends on the maker.
symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Rough idle or changed shifting until values are relearned
Readiness monitors reset
Often right after battery work
possible_causes: Battery disconnected, deeply discharged or replaced (likelihood: high)
Interrupted constant power feed to the module (fuse, wire, corrosion) (likelihood: medium)
Main relay drops out too early, memory not saved completely at shutdown (likelihood: low)
Internal memory defect (EEPROM/NVM) (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: engine control module, battery, control module power supply.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

title: DTC P0604 - Internal Control Module Random Access Memory (RAM) Error
problem_description: P0604 means the module's working memory (RAM) failed its self-test: a value written to a cell does not read back correctly, a built-in hardware test fails, error correction reports faults, or protected memory is written without permission. GM's engine module scans the whole RAM within 30 s of start-up and then keeps checking in the background, setting the code after repeated failures with the lamp in the first trip; Ford tests RAM during initialisation, the GM gateway with error correction at start (two trips). Unlike most memory codes, P0604 is used the same way by GM, Ford, Chrysler and Saab. Consequences depend on the module: a transmission module goes into limp mode with maximum line pressure and a fixed gear, an engine module may reduce power. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.

title: DTC P0605 - Internal Control Module Read Only Memory (ROM) Error

title: DTC P0606 - Control Module Processor
problem_description: P0606 means the module doubts the integrity of its own processor. title: DTC P0608 - Control Module VSS Output A
problem_description: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0608 concerns output A: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an open circuit or an internal driver fault, as CARB requires for output components. Output A is the first such output, usually the speedometer feed. If the speed sensor itself fails, P0500–P0503 set instead. No manufacturer table available to us gives thresholds; GM lists the code in older vehicles. On modern cars speed is shared over CAN, so the code mainly affects older vehicles with a hard-wired speedometer signal.

Cruise control not working
Odometer stops counting
Speed-dependent functions (steering, radio volume) disturbed
possible_causes: Short or open in the output line A to the receiving module (likelihood: high)
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver (likelihood: medium)
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground (likelihood: medium)
Internal driver fault in the module (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P060A - Internal Control Module Monitoring Processor Performance
problem_description: Electronic throttle systems use three levels: level 1 runs the engine, level 2 recalculates key values independently on the same processor, and level 3 is a separate monitoring processor that quizzes the main one and can shut down the throttle outputs. GM North America does not use P060A. Nissan (Rogue 2021) and Ford (Explorer 2.3 2025) fixed it by reprogramming – often there are no driving symptoms at all.

title: DTC P060B - Internal Control Module A/D Processing Performance
problem_description: The analog-to-digital converter turns every analog sensor voltage into a number, so a faulty converter can falsify many values at once. The module checks it by timing its start-up calibration (GM 6.6 L diesel: 0.30 s or longer is a fault), by converting fixed internal reference voltages (about 4.73–4.83 V must be read), by grounding a test channel that must then read near 0 V (Ford diesel: over 249 mV is a fault) and by comparing with a second converter. GM sets it in the first trip, Ford with the check engine and wrench lamps as a level 3 check; the module usually enters limp mode. Ford fixed an F-150 2.7 L case (with misfire codes) by reprogramming. GM also uses P060B in the brake module – then ABS warnings appear and the engine module is not the culprit. The old wording 'A and D' simply spelled out 'A/D'.

title: DTC P0612 - Fuel Injector Control Module Relay Control
problem_description: Some diesels have a separate injector driver module that is powered through a relay switched by the engine module – GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY with its injector driver unit, Ford's 6.0 L Power Stroke with its injector control module. title: DTC P0622 - Generator Field/F Terminal Circuit
problem_description: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0622 checks the F feedback: its duty cycle equals the field on-time, from which the module calculates alternator torque and raises idle under load. title: DTC P0623 - Generator Lamp Control Circuit
problem_description: P0623 concerns the control of the battery warning lamp by a module's output driver, not the alternator itself. Traditionally the regulator switches the lamp through terminal L; where a module switches it instead – GM's Saab 9-4X turns the lamp on 15 s after a charging code – it can monitor its lamp output for open or short circuits. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0623, so the description follows the principle of other lamp outputs. Under CARB a pure indicator lamp needs the check engine light only if other diagnostics depend on it, which is rarely the case. The lamp then never lights (not even at the bulb check) or stays on, and real charging faults may go unnoticed. The L line itself is P0621; the fuel cap lamp P0624 belongs to a different system.

title: DTC P0624 - Fuel Cap Lamp Control Circuit
problem_description: Despite its neighbours, P0624 has nothing to do with the alternator: it is the control circuit of the 'check fuel cap' warning lamp of the evaporative system. Ford's evaporative monitor lights such a lamp when, after refuelling, the tank cannot be pulled into vacuum – a gross leak or missing cap (P0457) – and turns it off once the cap is secured; not every vehicle has this lamp. The module driving the lamp (engine or body module, depending on the vehicle) can monitor its output for open or short circuits. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0624 itself. The lamp is only a hint; the leak is reported with the check engine light as P0455/P0457, so P0624 itself is practically emission neutral under CARB. The lamp then never lights or stays on, and a loose cap is no longer indicated.

title: DTC P062C - Internal Control Module Vehicle Speed Performance
problem_description: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. Vehicle speed feeds torque monitoring through cruise control, speed limiter and gear-dependent limits. P062C means the module's internal cross-check of vehicle speed fails – main software and monitoring determine it separately, for example from transmission output or wheel speeds, and the values disagree. Fix speed sensor codes P0500–P0503 first; a wrong tyre size or axle ratio in the module can also contribute.

title: DTC P062D - Fuel Injector Driver Circuit Performance Bank 1
problem_description: Direct-injection injectors (petrol and common-rail diesel) need a high boost voltage generated in the module to open fast; the module then holds them with pulsed battery voltage. Injectors then open late or not at all: misfires, rough running, loss of power or no start. GM uses only P062D, also on V8s. Single injector circuits are P0201 ff.

title: DTC P062F - Internal Control Module EEPROM Error
problem_description: Learned values, adaptations, counters and configuration are saved to non-volatile memory (EEPROM or flash-emulated NVM) when the module shuts down. P062F means this memory failed a check: GM and GM Europe test at start-up whether the last write at shutdown completed, GM's 6.6 L diesel checks a checksum per data block and whether sectors can be erased, Ford's diesel reports read, write or erase errors (5 s). Lamp behaviour varies: GM petrol engine modules after two trips, the Duramax 2014 and Saab 2.0 L turbo in the first trip, GM transmission modules and GM Europe's 1.6 L turbo without it. Most often the shutdown was interrupted – battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay dropping out too early. Learned values are lost and relearned. The code also appears in transmission and other modules.

title: DTC P0630 - VIN Not Programmed or Incompatible ECM/PCM
problem_description: Since model year 2005 CARB requires exactly one module to report the VIN to a scan tool, and reprogramming the VIN must erase all emission-related diagnostic data. P0630 means the engine module holds no valid VIN or one that does not fit. GM checks continuously whether every VIN position is a valid ASCII character (older tables: bytes 00 or FF count as empty), 250 ms, with the lamp in the first trip. At Ford the body module sends VIN, tyre circumference and axle ratio at every start, and P0630 sets while only default values are stored – so it covers more than the VIN; the 2023 diesel checks within 0.5 s. Hyundai requires writing the VIN after replacement; once written it cannot be changed. The engine runs normally; inspection stations may reject a missing VIN.

title: DTC P0633 - Immobilizer Key Not Programmed ECM/PCM
problem_description: The immobiliser couples the engine module to the immobiliser control module (GM body module, Chrysler SKIM/WCM) through a secret key and a challenge-response exchange – 'key' here means these security data, not the ignition key. P0633 means the engine module has not learned this secret key yet. At GM and Saab the code is set automatically whenever the engine module enters learn mode, for example as a new part, and clears after a successful learn and engine start; it is only a real fault if learn mode does not end, often because the engine fails to start for another reason. Chrysler calls it 'SKIM secret key not stored in PCM' and fixed false settings on the 2012–13 Grand Voyager 2.8 diesel by software. The engine does not start or dies after one or two seconds; the security lamp, not the check engine light, comes on.

title: DTC P0634 - Control Module Internal Temperature A Too High
problem_description: The module measures its own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor and sets P0634 when it overheats. In practice this concerns mainly transmission modules mounted in or on the gearbox, such as GM's 6T70/6T75 and 6L units with the module in the valve body, surrounded by transmission fluid. GM sets it at 142 °C or more for 5 s (Saab 9-4X: 146 °C), or at 50 °C or more with system voltage of 18 V or higher for 2 s, because overvoltage heats the output stages. The Saab 9-4X then goes into limp mode with only reverse and 5th gear, manual shifting disabled and maximum line pressure; GM's table rates it without the check engine light. Check transmission overtemperature (P0218) first, then fluid level and cooler, engine cooling and charging voltage. Faults of the internal temperature sensor circuit are P0666–P0669.

The compressor then does not engage or runs constantly.

title: DTC P064A - Fuel Pump Control Module A
problem_description: Demand-controlled fuel systems drive the pump through a separate pump control module; the engine module sets the target and reads its status back. P064A means this module reports an internal fault. Ford petrol engines encode the status as a duty cycle on a monitor line – 30 % (±4 %) means internal driver fault, 20 % invalid data (P025B), no signal U0109 – and set the code after 2–5 s; Ford's 2023 diesel checks the period of the monitor signal (0–1.2 s, 0.5 s). GM's pump module sets P064A when its output stage exceeds 150 °C (3 of 15 samples), with the lamp after two trips; Ford petrol stores it without the lamp. Pump output may be reduced or switched off, so low fuel pressure, stalling or a no-start can follow. A stiff, worn pump drawing high current can overheat the module.

title: DTC P064C - Glow Plug Control Module 1
problem_description: On diesels a glow plug control module switches the glow plugs (at Ford also the DEF heaters) with semiconductor switches, diagnoses itself and reports to the engine module. title: DTC P064D - Internal Control Module O2 Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1
problem_description: Wide-band oxygen sensors need a pump current control; inside the engine module a dedicated chip (ASIC, for example Bosch's CJ125 family) regulates it, measures lambda, diagnoses sensor wiring and heater, and talks to the main processor via SPI. P064D means this chip for bank 1 sensor 1 does not work correctly or its messages are invalid. Ford validates the SPI communication continuously and sets P064D/P064E after 10 s at 11–18 V with the sensor heater working; an internal chip fault adds Ford's P1646/P1647. GM (wide-band engines such as the 3.0 L twin turbo, 2018–2025) evaluates two error counters from the chip and sets the code at 128 of 160 samples (about 4 s), more than 20 s after start-up, with the lamp after two trips. Fuel control then runs open loop and oxygen sensor monitors are disabled – fuel consumption and emissions rise. Faults in the sensor or wiring can also push the chip into an invalid state.

Voltage dips or software (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P064F - Unauthorized Software/Calibration Detected
problem_description: P064F means the module has found that its software or calibration is not the version released by the manufacturer, or fails an authenticity check (signature, checksum, security keys). CARB requires manufacturers to protect calibrations against changes without special tools and to report calibration IDs and checksums. GM's 2025 engine modules set it when the embedded message authentication table for secured bus messages is invalid, with the lamp in the first trip; chassis modules also check missing key storage or wrong key-slot configuration. Chrysler fixed P064F on the 2017 Ram 3500–5500 chassis cab 6.7 L Cummins by reprogramming – so it is not only about tuning. Typical triggers are tuning software, an interrupted or wrong reflash, a module from another vehicle, or a module replaced without learning its security keys. Programming released software usually clears it.

title: DTC P0662 - Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit High Bank 1
problem_description: The intake manifold tuning valve switches the manifold length or plenum connection with engine speed (more torque low, more power high); it is not the runner or swirl flap (IMRC, P2004 ff). P0662 means a short to voltage in the bank 1 control circuit: with the driver on, the low-side line should be pulled to ground, but the voltage stays high (0.5 Ω or less to positive); the driver protects itself and the valve is not actuated. GM's engines with this valve (low-side driver) check with ignition voltage of at least 11 V and the engine above 400 rpm and set the code after 40 of 50 samples (about 0.6 s), with the check engine light after two trips. Ford does not use P0662. The valve stays in its rest position, with a power loss around the switch-over speed.
symptoms: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Loss of power in part of the rev range
Actuator does not click when switching
possible_causes: Control wire shorted to battery or supply voltage (harness) (likelihood: high)
Actuator winding shorted (very low resistance, overcurrent) (likelihood: medium)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector between supply and control pin (likelihood: medium)
Output driver in the engine module faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0662 (Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit High Bank 1).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: intake manifold tuning valve, valve actuator, actuator wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Control wire shorted to battery or supply voltage (harness) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Actuator winding shorted (very low resistance, overcurrent) (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P0666 - Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit
problem_description: Control modules measure their own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor to protect output stages (overtemperature is P0634) and, in GM transmission modules, as a substitute for fluid temperature. In GM's 6T70/6T75 and related automatics the sensor sits in the transmission module inside the valve body, with no external wiring – so the repair is practically always the module or valve body assembly. P0666 is the general circuit fault of this sensor A. No manufacturer table available to us uses P0666 itself – GM splits the circuit faults into low (P0668) and high (P0669), plausibility is P0667. Expect a warning lamp and, in a transmission module, changed shift quality because a substitute temperature is used.

Changed shift quality (substitute value)
Possibly transmission fluid temperature codes
possible_causes: Module faulty internally (temperature sensor or measuring circuit) (likelihood: high)

Supply or ground problems of the module (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission control module, control module internal temperature sensor.

Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

title: DTC P066A - Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
problem_description: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P066A means the circuit to the cylinder 1 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag a circuit impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples at 100 ms) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off, so plug 1 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow. A plug shorted internally is the usual cause; a wrong plug type is another.
symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp
Harder cold start, especially in frost
Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start
Possibly blown glow system fuse
possible_causes: Glow plug cylinder 1 shorted internally (element against body) (likelihood: high)
Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (block, bracket) (likelihood: medium)
Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating) (likelihood: low)
Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM 3.0 L 2020) (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P066A (Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: glow plug, glow plug wiring, glow plug control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Glow plug cylinder 1 shorted internally (element against body) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (block, bracket) (likelihood: medium).

title: DTC P0670 - Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit/Open
problem_description: In today's J2012 meaning P0670 is the electrical check of the activation line from the engine module to glow plug control module 1 for an open circuit; a short to ground is P0383, a short to voltage P0384, and serial communication between the modules P0683/P0684. On Bosch systems (Saab 2.2 TiD and EDC16) the engine module switches this line, detects an open load with the output off and a short to voltage with it on, and also compares the glow module's diagnostic feedback, which must switch inversely – Saab reports all line faults under P0670. GM's LB7/LLY Duramax (2004–05) used P0670 in an older meaning for glow module performance (50 of 100 samples, two trips). No current GM or Ford table uses it. If the line fails, no plug heats: hard or no cold start in frost, smoke and rough running.
symptoms: Check engine light on
Glow plug lamp behaves implausibly (stays off or on)
Hard or no cold start in frost, since no plug heats
Smoke and rough running after a cold start
possible_causes: Wire or connector between engine and glow module open or corroded (bent pin, contact tension) (likelihood: high)
Glow module faulty (input open) or without supply or ground (fuse, terminal 30) (likelihood: medium)
Control line shorted (makers reporting all line faults under P0670, e.g. Saab) (likelihood: medium)
Output driver in the engine module faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0670 (Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit/Open).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: glow plug control module, glow plug control circuit, engine control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Wire or connector between engine and glow module open or corroded (bent pin, contact tension) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Glow module faulty (input open) or without supply or ground (fuse, terminal 30) (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard
