title: DTC P0671 - Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Circuit/Open
problem_description: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P0671 means the load circuit of the cylinder 1 glow plug is open while glowing. Thresholds: GM engine-module drivers 200 kΩ or more (two trips), GM's L5P glow module less than 4.0 A at over 6 V, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke less than 1 A for about 1 s. Older GM systems (LB7/LLY, LML) report open and short under this one code. Chrysler advises checking the main B+ feed and ground of the glow module first when several cylinder codes appear together.
symptoms: Check engine light (GM also glow plug lamp)
Harder cold start in low temperatures
Rough idle, knocking and white or blue smoke after a cold start
Often no symptoms when warm
possible_causes: Glow plug cylinder 1 burnt out (element open) (likelihood: high)
Plug connector loose or corroded, terminal nut loose, wire broken (likelihood: medium)
Glow module supply or ground (several cylinder codes at once) (likelihood: medium)
Glow module or driver faulty, or software (GM 3.0 L 2020) (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0671 (Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Circuit/Open).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: glow plug, glow plug wiring, glow plug control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Glow plug cylinder 1 burnt out (element open) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Plug connector loose or corroded, terminal nut loose, wire broken (likelihood: medium).

title: DTC P068C - Cylinder 7 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
problem_description: Modern diesel glow systems switch each glow plug through its own power semiconductor (in a glow plug module or the engine module), so current and faults can be measured per plug; a faulty channel is switched off. CARB requires glow plugs to be checked for correct current and voltage drop and, since model year 2010, a single plug outside specification to be detected and named. P068C means the circuit to the cylinder 7 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. GM's engine-module drivers flag an impedance to ground below 0.11 Ω (10 of 20 samples) with the check engine and glow plug lamps after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks during heating for more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s. The channel is switched off and plug 7 no longer heats – harder cold starts and white smoke follow.
symptoms: Check engine and glow plug lamp
Harder cold start, especially in frost
Rough running and white smoke right after a cold start
possible_causes: Glow plug cylinder 7 shorted internally (element against body) (likelihood: high)
Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (likelihood: medium)
Wrong plug type (resistance or voltage rating) (likelihood: low)
Driver in the glow or engine module faulty, or software (GM bulletins) (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P068C (Cylinder 7 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: glow plug, glow plug wiring, glow plug control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Glow plug cylinder 7 shorted internally (element against body) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Plug wire insulation damaged and shorted to ground (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

title: DTC P0690 - ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit High
problem_description: The engine module switches its main relay coil to ground (control circuit), reads the switched voltage back on a sense line and keeps the relay on briefly after ignition off to save learned values. P0690 means the sense voltage is too high: voltage is present although the relay has been off for 2 s – a welded or sticking contact, or external voltage fed in through a short – or, on some systems, overvoltage above 18 V with the relay on. GM sets it at 4 V or more with the relay off, in 50 of 63 samples at 100 ms, lamp after two trips; GM Europe's 2.0 L turbo above 2 V with the relay off or above 18 V with it on, for 2 s, and advises fixing other short-to-voltage codes first. Modules, fans or pumps may keep running after switch-off and the battery drains overnight.
symptoms: Check engine light
Module, fan or pumps keep running after ignition off
Battery drains overnight
possible_causes: Relay contact sticking or welded (likelihood: high)
Short to voltage on the sense or load line (external feed from another component) (likelihood: medium)
Control wire shorted to ground (relay permanently on) (likelihood: medium)
Overvoltage from the alternator regulator (where the 18 V limit applies) (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0690 (ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: ecm power relay, relay control circuit, engine control module.

title: DTC P06A0 - Variable A/C Compressor Control Circuit
problem_description: Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their swash-plate stroke via an electric control valve: a PWM current sets the crankcase pressure and thus the output. Where the engine module drives this valve (Ford's 'EVDC' compressors 2013–2019), it monitors the circuit; where the climate control module drives it (Hyundai, VW/Audi, GM), faults appear in that module instead. title: DTC P06B8 - Internal Control Module Non-Volatile Random Access Memory (NVRAM) Error
problem_description: Non-volatile RAM keeps its content without power; among other things it stores the permanent fault codes CARB requires, which cannot be cleared with a scan tool. Ford sets P06B8 when the checksum of this permanent-code memory is wrong; a common companion is P068A (main relay dropped out too early, memory write incomplete). Ford's commercial and propane variants list it with or without the check engine light depending on the vehicle; Ford's 2023 diesel table misprints it as 'P068B'. GM and Saab do not use P06B8. Typical causes are interrupted shutdowns (battery disconnected, voltage dips), software faults and, rarely, a memory defect. After a software check, clearing and an ignition cycle with normal shutdown often resolve it.

Often no driving symptoms
Possibly P068A as well

Weak battery or poor ground (likelihood: medium)
Memory defect in the module (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P06C5 - Cylinder 1 Glow Plug Incorrect
problem_description: A glow plug has no identification; the control unit recognises its type only from its electrical behaviour – cold resistance at switch-on and how resistance rises during heating (R = U/I). A Beru patent describes how steel and ceramic plugs are told apart this way so the right heating profile is used and a wrong or mixed type is reported. A low-voltage plug on an 11 V control burns out, an 11 V plug on a low-voltage control glows too weakly. GM uses 'incorrect' for any resistance outside the window: the 2025 diesels check 0.22–2.00 Ω (15 of 25 samples, two trips), the L5P glow module a ramp-dependent window. P06C5 reports this for cylinder 1. VW's 2.0 TDI (Jetta, Golf, Passat 2011–13) checks the type 2 s after ignition on – starting during that time caused false codes from the voltage dip, fixed with new glow module software.

title: DTC P06D1 - Internal Control Module Ignition Coil Control Performance
problem_description: On ignition systems where the coils are driven through a separate driver chip inside the engine module, P06D1 reports that this internal coil control does not work correctly. title: DTC P06DA - Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit/Open
problem_description: A switchable or variable oil pump saves fuel by lowering its output at part load; a solenoid valve sets the stage. GM and Ford design it so the pump runs at full output, i.e. high pressure, when the valve is unpowered – the safe default – and at the low stage when powered. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander uses the same code. The engine is not at risk, the pump just can no longer be regulated.

title: DTC P06DD - Engine Oil Pressure Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
problem_description: A switchable oil pump changes its output via a solenoid valve; unpowered it delivers high pressure. title: DTC P06DF - Glow Plug Control Module 1 Memory Checksum Error
problem_description: A diesel glow plug control module has its own microcontroller. On power-up it forms a checksum over its memory and compares it with the stored value; P06DF means they differ, so the module's program or data cannot be trusted. Ford's 2023 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke list P06DF among the glow module checks, run at power-up and flagged on a RAM checksum mismatch after about 1 s. GM's L5P performs the same check on ROM (4.5 s, two trips) but reports it as P064C. CARB treats the module as a 'smart device' whose internal faults need not be pinpointed, so this is extra diagnosis by the manufacturer. The usual remedy is reprogramming or replacing the module; until then preheating may be missing.

title: DTC P06E0 - Cylinder 11 Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
problem_description: Diesel glow systems switch each plug through its own power semiconductor and switch off a faulty channel; CARB requires single-plug detection from model year 2010. P06E0 means the circuit to the cylinder 11 glow plug is shorted to ground or draws overcurrent. For cylinders 1–8, GM's engine-module drivers flag below 0.11 Ω to ground after two trips, and Ford's 2023 Power Stroke more than 22 A for 0.3 s or 20–22 A for 2 s while heating. The channel is switched off and the plug stays cold; the other plugs keep working. An internally shorted plug or a chafed wire is the usual cause. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it needs at least 11 cylinders, and the only US OBD II diesel above eight, VW's Touareg V10 TDI, has ten; the description follows cylinders 1–8.

title: DTC P06E4 - Control Module Wake-up Circuit Performance
problem_description: Control modules are woken by a dedicated wake-up line or a network wake-up – at ignition on, when a charging cable is plugged in, or on a timer for engine-off diagnostics and battery management. P06E4 means this wake-up signal is implausible: the module wakes too late or not at all, stays awake, or the line state does not match the network status. In practice the code appears mainly on hybrids: FCA fixes it on the Pacifica plug-in hybrid and the Wrangler 4xe with module software, where it remained as a permanent code that blocked emission inspections; GM's hybrid integration module lists it as a fault bundle. No manufacturer publishes thresholds or timing.

Possibly battery drain (module stays awake)

Wake-up line or connector open or shorted (likelihood: medium)

title: DTC P06EA - NOx Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
problem_description: A modern NOx sensor is a smart sensor: a ceramic sensing element with pump cells and heater plus its own control unit with a microcontroller, which regulates the pump currents, calculates NOx and oxygen and sends them to the engine module over CAN. P06EA means this control unit of sensor 1 (before the SCR catalyst) reports an internal fault – its self-tests of RAM and ROM or EEPROM checksums fail – so the electronics, not the sensing element, are at fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: Ford's 2023 diesels run exactly these checks continuously, with a fault after 5 s, but report them as P2200; GM uses the P2200 family and U029D/U029E. The NOx value is then invalid, so SCR dosing runs on a model or stops, a warning appears and, depending on market, a countdown to a start lock.

title: DTC P06ED - Engine RPM Output Circuit Low
problem_description: The engine module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer, transmission or body-builder modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P06ED means this output is too low, typically shorted to ground, so it can no longer switch high. It is the counterpart of P0654 (open circuit) and P06EE (high). CARB requires output circuits to be checked; the signal is emission-relevant only if a receiving module uses it for emission functions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB, the component and P0654. The tachometer then reads zero or jumps, and modules using the signal lose it, while the engine runs normally.

title: DTC P06F3 - Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit High

title: DTC P0710 - Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit
problem_description: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0710 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not separate low and high. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag 0.1 V or less or 4.7 V or more, light the MIL after two consecutive trips and use 80 °C as substitute. Ford's 2023 diesels use P0710 alongside P0712/P0713 for open and short circuits, without MIL, after 5–12 s, substituting coolant temperature. GM uses only the split codes. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071F means the signal of mode switch B is above its upper limit – an open circuit or short to positive. Mode B then cannot be selected. The opposite is P071E.
symptoms: Mode B cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule
possible_causes: Wire or connector to the button open (likelihood: high)
Button open internally (likelihood: medium)
Signal wire shorted to positive (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P071F (Transmission Mode Switch B Circuit High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission mode switch, switch wiring, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Wire or connector to the button open (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Button open internally (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P0720 - Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit
problem_description: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0720 is the general circuit code. Ford also uses it for 'no signal': while engine and turbine speed show the vehicle moving, the sensor reports under 100–200 rpm for 5–30 s; ZF's 6HP26 in Ford vehicles flags an open or short after 0.6 s. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag an impossible 255 km/h or 0 km/h while driving and light the MIL after two trips, substituting the other sensor. GM does not use P0720 but P0722. Speedometer and cruise control may fail, often with a vehicle speed code as well.
symptoms: Speedometer drops out or jumps
Warning lamp, limp mode or fixed gear
Harsh shifts, cruise control not working
possible_causes: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted) (likelihood: high)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector) (likelihood: high)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel (likelihood: medium)
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: output speed sensor, sensor wiring, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2.5 hours

If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector) (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P0723 - Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Intermittent
problem_description: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. title: DTC P0724 - Brake Switch B Circuit High
problem_description: Brake switch B is the brake signal to the transmission module or a second brake switch channel, used to release the converter clutch, adapt shift strategy on grades and cancel cruise control. Low and high describe the signal voltage, and what that means depends on polarity: GM's converter clutch brake switch is closed at rest (12 V), while Saab's Trionic 8 sees 12 V when braking. Detection is always a plausibility check against driving: the brake reads applied during accelerations or never applied during decelerations. P0724 means the signal stays high. For GM that reads as brake never applied: 2006 transmission modules flag it after eight decelerations without a brake signal of at least 2 s, without MIL. Saab's Trionic 8 flags a brake light signal that reads on while accelerating from 3 to 40 km/h, four times, and disables cruise control. The opposite is P0719.
symptoms: Cruise control cannot be activated or switches off
Unusual shifting, converter clutch behaviour changed
No downshift on uphill grades (Subaru)
Brake lights stay off or on
possible_causes: Brake light switch sticking or misadjusted (likelihood: high)
Signal wire shorted to positive (Saab T8) or switch permanently closed (GM) (likelihood: medium)
Retrofitted trailer or LED lights feeding back (likelihood: low)
Module input faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0724 (Brake Switch B Circuit High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: brake switch, brake switch wiring, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Brake light switch sticking or misadjusted (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Signal wire shorted to positive (Saab T8) or switch permanently closed (GM) (likelihood: medium).

title: DTC P0725 - Engine Speed Input Circuit
problem_description: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0725 is the general fault of this input; with CAN it means the engine module marks its speed value as invalid. Saab's Aisin transmissions and a 2006 GM table set it after about 4 s, the GM table with immediate MIL. A Saab bulletin notes that behind P0725 there is always a crankshaft or camshaft sensor code in the engine module (P0016, P0335–P0339) – so read the engine module first. Limp mode follows; a completely missing CAN message is U0100.
symptoms: Transmission warning lamp, possibly check engine light
Torque converter clutch locked out
Harsh shifts or limp mode
Often an engine code (crankshaft sensor) as well
possible_causes: Crankshaft or camshaft sensor fault in the engine module (speed invalid there) (likelihood: high)
CAN fault between engine and transmission module (wiring, termination, connector) (likelihood: medium)
Engine module software or fault (likelihood: low)
Transmission module faulty (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: engine speed signal, can bus, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours

title: DTC P0729 - Gear 6 Incorrect Ratio
problem_description: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0729 concerns sixth gear. Saab's Aisin six-speed also checks whether the actual ratio matches fourth or fifth – the sixth gear clutch is not holding and the box drops into another gear. Ford stores it only if the fault does not fit a particular solenoid (otherwise P0751 ff). On GM manual transmissions (LT4) it checks the gear position sensor instead.
symptoms: Slipping or flare in sixth gear, engine speed higher than expected
Harsh or delayed shifts
Limp mode (Aisin: second gear and reverse only), transmission warning
Check engine light depending on manufacturer
possible_causes: Fluid level too low or fluid worn or contaminated (likelihood: high)
Clutch for sixth gear worn (linings, piston seal) (likelihood: high)
Sticking shift or pressure valve, leaking valve body gasket, blocked passages (likelihood: medium)
GM manual transmissions only: gear position sensor faulty or not learned (likelihood: medium)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0729 (Gear 6 Incorrect Ratio).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission clutches, transmission valve body, transmission fluid, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-14 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Fluid level too low or fluid worn or contaminated (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Clutch for sixth gear worn (linings, piston seal) (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P072A - Stuck in Neutral
problem_description: Ford's DPS6 dry dual-clutch transmission moves its gears with two electrically driven shift drums whose position is read by Hall sensors: drum A shifts 1st, 3rd and 5th, drum B reverse, 2nd, 4th and 6th. Ford's 2012 summary lists 'stuck in gear' codes for each drum: the module commands the drum out of a gear, but the gear stays engaged. It gives no thresholds or MIL rating. P072A means the transmission stays in neutral although a gear is commanded – no drive. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the DPS6 reports drum position faults under its own codes. On dual-clutch or automated manuals a drum or fork would fail to engage a gear, on planetary automatics clutch pressure would be missing. The opposite is P073D.
symptoms: Transmission stays in one gear, no further shifts
Limp mode, transmission warning
Clunking or blocking when shifting
possible_causes: Shift fork or synchronizer for this gear sticking (likelihood: medium)
Shift drum A motor, Hall position sensing or driver faulty (likelihood: medium)
Transmission module (likelihood: low)
On planetary automatics: clutch or brake not releasing (sticking valve) (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P072A (Stuck in Neutral).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: shift drum, shift fork, shift drum motor, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-10 hours

title: DTC P0730 - Incorrect Gear Ratio

Ford and newer GM step automatics use gear-specific or clutch valve codes instead. Check fluid level and condition first.

title: DTC P0731 - Gear 1 Incorrect Ratio
problem_description: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0731 concerns first gear. A 2006 GM table uses a tighter 4 % limit here and caps output speed at 1260 rpm; Saab's 2002 9-5 flags 3 % with the brake released. With a one-way clutch in first, slip shows as slipping when pulling away. On GM manual transmissions it checks the gear position sensor instead.
symptoms: Slipping or flare in first gear, engine speed higher than expected
Harsh or delayed shifts
Limp mode (Aisin: second gear and reverse only), transmission warning
Check engine light depending on manufacturer

title: DTC P0737 - TCM Engine Speed Output Circuit
problem_description: Some transmission modules pass an engine speed signal on to other devices such as a tachometer over a wire of their own. CARB requires output circuits to be checked. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0737–P0739 – engine speed is shared over CAN today; the description follows CARB and the engine module's own speed output (P0654), which sends, for example, two pulses per revolution. P0737 is the general circuit fault of this output; low and high are P0738/P0739. Not to be confused with the engine speed input at the transmission module (P0725 ff). A tachometer or dependent display then reads wrong or nothing, while driving is usually unaffected.
symptoms: Tachometer or dependent display not working or wrong
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer
Usually no effect on driving
possible_causes: Wire to the receiver open or shorted (likelihood: high)
Receiver (e.g. instrument cluster) shorted internally (likelihood: medium)
Connector corroded (likelihood: medium)
Driver stage in the transmission module faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0737 (TCM Engine Speed Output Circuit).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: engine speed output circuit, tachometer, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Wire to the receiver open or shorted (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P077A - Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Loss of Direction Signal
problem_description: Some transmissions use an output shaft speed sensor that also reports direction of rotation: in a GM patent two offset Hall elements send one pulse per tooth whose width encodes forward or reverse. title: DTC P07B2 - Transmission Park Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit/Open
problem_description: With electronic gear selection the park position sensor/switch reports the park request or position. On GM's shift-by-wire selectors (2017 LaCrosse, XT4/XT5, Bolt EV, later SUVs and pickups) it is the P button, read by two redundant analog sensors A and B with separate 'released' and 'pressed' voltage zones. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM covers an open analog circuit under its low and high codes (P07B3/P07B4), which CARB allows when an open cannot be told apart from an out-of-range value. problem_description: These low/high codes are a purely electrical check of the sensor's signal voltage at the module and run even with the vehicle at rest – unlike the circuit, range, no-signal and intermittent codes, which evaluate speed while driving. Low means a short to ground, high a short to supply or, depending on the circuit, an open. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code, and no production transmission with a third input speed sensor was found. The expected logic follows GM's sensor A check (below 0.25 V); the remaining codes for sensor C are P07F1 ff.
symptoms: Check engine light (GM after one trip)
Limp mode, harsh shifts, no converter lock-up
Adaption frozen
possible_causes: Signal or supply wire shorted to ground (chafing at the case) (likelihood: high)
Sensor shorted internally (likelihood: medium)
Oil or moisture in the connector (likelihood: medium)
Module input faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P07C3 (Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor C Circuit Low).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: input speed sensor, sensor wiring, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-4 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Signal or supply wire shorted to ground (chafing at the case) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Sensor shorted internally (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

title: DTC P07CB - Transmission Fluid Thermostat Performance
problem_description: Many automatics have a thermostat in the fluid cooler circuit or a coolant-to-oil heat exchanger: a BMW patent describes a wax thermostat that bypasses the cooler until about 76 °C, a Ford patent a heat exchanger that warms transmission fluid from the coolant after a cold start. P07CB means this thermostat does not work as expected: fluid warms up too slowly (stuck open) or overheats (stuck closed). No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; GM checks fluid warm-up under the temperature sensor code P0711 (below 15 °C after the warm-up time, two trips). The check works like CARB's engine thermostat monitor (P0128). Slow warm-up raises consumption and delays converter lock-up; overheating ages fluid quickly.
symptoms: Check engine or transmission warning lamp
Converter clutch applies late, higher consumption
Fluid overheating warning
possible_causes: Transmission fluid thermostat stuck open or closed (likelihood: high)
Fluid temperature sensor drifting (likelihood: medium)
Cooler lines or heat exchanger blocked or leaking (likelihood: medium)
Very cold weather or short trips (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P07CB (Transmission Fluid Thermostat Performance).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission fluid thermostat, transmission fluid cooler, transmission fluid temperature sensor, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Transmission fluid thermostat stuck open or closed (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P07CC - Transmission Mode Switch C Circuit Low
problem_description: Transmission mode switches select alternative shift programs such as sport, winter or tow/haul; the J2012 family runs from A (P071A–P071C) and B (P071D–P071F) to C (base code P078F), D and E. No manufacturer document available to us uses switches C to E; GM reads its analog mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, two trips) and newer drive mode selectors under P05D0–P05D3. P07CC means the signal of mode switch C is below its lower limit – a short to ground or a button stuck against ground. The opposite is P07CD.
symptoms: Mode C cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal program
possible_causes: Signal wire shorted to ground (likelihood: high)
Button stuck pressed (switching to ground) (likelihood: medium)
Moisture or dirt in the button (likelihood: medium)
Control module (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P07CC (Transmission Mode Switch C Circuit Low).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission mode switch, switch wiring, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Signal wire shorted to ground (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Button stuck pressed (switching to ground) (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.

No manufacturer document available to us uses switches C to E; GM reads its analog mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, two trips) and newer drive mode selectors under P05D0–P05D3. P07D3 means the signal of mode switch E is above its upper limit – an open circuit or a short to positive. The opposite is P07D2.
symptoms: Mode E cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal program
possible_causes: Wire or connector to the button open (likelihood: high)
Button open internally (likelihood: medium)
Signal wire shorted to positive (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P07D3 (Transmission Mode Switch E Circuit High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission mode switch, switch wiring, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Wire or connector to the button open (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Button open internally (likelihood: medium).
Clear diagnostic trouble codes with scanner after component repair and perform a verification test drive.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P07D7 - Stuck in Gear 8
problem_description: P07D7 means gear 8 cannot be disengaged: the module commands a shift out of 8th, but the transmission stays in it. It is the counterpart to P07D8, where gear 8 cannot be engaged. The only documented user is Maserati's eight-speed dual-clutch gearbox in the MC20 (from model year 2023), whose bulletin lists it next to the other 'Stuck in Gear' codes: hydraulic actuators move the shift forks, and a fork that does not reach neutral is reported. The repair path there first runs a service fast-learn with valve flushing and new adaptation, then records system pressure – it should hold 20–30 bar; drops below 5 bar point to the mechatronic unit, a stable pressure to the gearbox itself. No thresholds or trip counts are published.
symptoms: Transmission stays in gear 8 and will not downshift
Weak take-off after stopping
Transmission warning, limp mode
possible_causes: Shift fork actuator or shift valve sticking (contamination) (likelihood: high)
System pressure low or unstable (mechatronic pressure valve) (likelihood: medium)
Shift fork, synchronizer or gear damaged (likelihood: medium)
Fluid or filter contaminated (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P07D7 (Stuck in Gear 8).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: shift fork actuator, transmission mechatronics, shift fork, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-12 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Shift fork actuator or shift valve sticking (contamination) (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P07D9 - Gear 8 Incorrect Ratio
problem_description: A ratio code compares input or turbine speed divided by output speed with the ratio of the commanded gear; a slipping clutch or the wrong gear trips it. Ford's summaries describe the check (over 30 rpm off for more than 1.8 s, three times) for gears 1–6 only; its 10-speed bulletins show gears 7–10 as P076F, P07D9, P07F6 and P07F7. P07D9 covers 8th gear. Ford's 10R80 (F-150, Mustang, Ranger, Expedition and others) and 10R140 (2020 Super Duty) list it in bulletins on harsh or delayed shifts, caused by adaptive learning, sticking valve-body valves or a migrating sleeve in a clutch cylinder. Nissan's nine-speed Frontier and Titan set it with the MIL on; a Stellantis bulletin pairs it with P0731 on low-mileage vehicles with wrong factory adaptives. Hyundai's eight-speeds and GM's 10-speed do not use it.
symptoms: Slipping or flaring engine speed in gear 8
Harsh or delayed shifts
Check engine or transmission warning lamp
Gear 8 locked out, higher rpm at cruise
possible_causes: Clutch slipping or hydraulic leak (Ford 10R: migrating sleeve in the CDF clutch cylinder) (likelihood: high)
Shift adaptives wrong or not learned (likelihood: high)
Sticking valve in the valve body (likelihood: medium)
Fluid level low or fluid degraded (likelihood: medium)
Turbine or output speed sensor signal wrong (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P07D9 (Gear 8 Incorrect Ratio).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission clutches, transmission valve body, transmission fluid, transmission control module.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-14 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Clutch slipping or hydraulic leak (Ford 10R: migrating sleeve in the CDF clutch cylinder) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Shift adaptives wrong or not learned (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P07DA - 6-7 Shift
problem_description: Shift codes check the gear change itself: the module compares the commanded change with the speed trace and flags a shift that takes too long, does not happen, flares or binds up two clutches. title: DTC P07DC - Incorrect Shift from Gear 1
problem_description: The series 'Incorrect Shift from Gear N' (P07DC–P07E3 for gears 1–8, P07FA and P07FD for 9 and 10) covers a shift that leaves the starting gear but lands in a gear other than the commanded target – a skipped or overshot gear. A module can see this after the shift because the measured ratio matches the wrong gear. No manufacturer document available to us uses the series: Ford assigns such patterns to the shift solenoid that caused them (P0751 ff), newer GM automatics report clutch pressure valve codes. P07DC starts from gear 1. It differs from P0731 (wrong ratio while in gear 1, a slipping clutch), P072C (gear 1 cannot be left) and P0781 (the shift itself takes too long or flares). Detection, MIL and trip count therefore follow only by analogy from CARB's functional check and Ford's ratio and shift completion checks.
symptoms: Wrong or skipped gear when shifting out of gear 1
Harsh shift or engine speed jump
Transmission warning, possibly limp mode in a fixed gear
possible_causes: Shift or pressure control valve sticking in the valve body (likelihood: high)
Clutch or brake pack worn or leaking (likelihood: medium)
Fluid low or contaminated (likelihood: medium)
Wrong adaptives or software (likelihood: medium)
Turbine or output speed signal wrong (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0800 - Transfer Case Control System (MIL Request)

The engine module only stores P0800; the actual fault – often C, U or manufacturer codes – sits in the transfer case module and needs a scan tool that addresses it. CARB requires monitoring of an electronic transfer case only where it feeds other diagnostics, for example the 4WD-low signal that GM uses as an enable condition; this is why most transfer case modules never request the MIL and P0800 hardly appears in manufacturer documents. A GM bulletin for 2020–23 trucks with 'Service 4WD' and the MIL points to wiring and terminal contact at the transfer case.
symptoms: Check engine lamp on
'Service 4WD' or similar warning
All-wheel drive or low range cannot be selected
possible_causes: Fault in the transfer case system stored in its module (shift motor, sensor, clutch) (likelihood: high)
Wiring or connector at the transfer case (terminal tension, corrosion) (likelihood: medium)
Transfer case module software (likelihood: medium)
Transfer case module faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0800 (Transfer Case Control System (MIL Request)).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transfer case control module, engine control module, transfer case wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Fault in the transfer case system stored in its module (shift motor, sensor, clutch) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Wiring or connector at the transfer case (terminal tension, corrosion) (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

title: DTC P0801 - Reverse Inhibit Control Circuit/Open
problem_description: On GM manual gearboxes (Tremec T56/TR6060 in Corvette, Camaro, CTS-V and ATS-V) the engine module drives a solenoid that blocks reverse while the car moves forward. P0801 means its control circuit is open. GM's tables describe the check: the low-side driver's internal diagnosis flags an open line with at least 9 V and the engine above 250 rpm, 20 failures in 25 samples of 250 ms – about 6 s; in 2006 a 5 s comparison of commanded and actual driver state. GM rates it type C, emissions-neutral and without MIL, from 2019 with a 'service vehicle soon' note. Depending on how it fails, reverse cannot be engaged or is no longer blocked. The title was updated to the current J2012 wording with '/Open'.

Reverse no longer blocked
Service note in the driver display, usually no MIL

Harness between engine module and gearbox damaged (likelihood: medium)
Engine module driver faulty (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0802 - Transmission Control System MIL Request Circuit/Open
problem_description: On older vehicles with a separate transmission module and no MIL message on the CAN bus, the transmission module signals 'MIL on' over its own wire to the engine module. P0802 checks this wire for an open circuit. GM's Duramax tables of 2004 and 2005 (Allison 1000) describe it: at key-on the transmission module briefly pulls the line active like a bulb check; if the engine module sees no off-to-on transition between 0.125 and 7 s after ignition, the line is treated as open – type B, MIL after two trips. Only then is P0700 evaluated. The wire itself must be monitored because an open line would stop transmission emission faults from lighting the MIL. Newer vehicles send the request over CAN, where faults appear as U codes.

Transmission faults no longer light the MIL
Usually no change in driving

Transmission module without power or ground (fuse, relay) (likelihood: medium)
Module output or input faulty (likelihood: low)
Wrong or retrofitted transmission module without this line (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: transmission control module, engine control module, mil request wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2 hours

title: DTC P0803 - Upshift/Skip Shift Solenoid Control Circuit
problem_description: GM's skip-shift (CAGS) on manual gearboxes such as the T56 and TR6060 uses an engine-module solenoid in the shifter housing that, at light load and low speed blocks the way from 1st into 2nd and 3rd so the driver shifts 1 to 4 – a measure for fuel economy ratings; the 1-4 lamp (P0804) shows it. P0803 means the solenoid control circuit is open. GM's tables check the low-side driver while it is off: too low a voltage or over 200 kΩ to ground, with at least 9 V and over 250 rpm, 5 of 6 samples of 250 ms (2019 LT5: 20 of 25), type B with the MIL after two trips; shorts are P080C and P080D. An open circuit leaves the solenoid unpowered, so 1 to 2 always works. 'Skip-shift eliminators' with the wrong resistance are a frequent cause.

1-4 lockout no longer works (1-2 always possible)
Otherwise no change in driving

Connector at the gearbox loose or corroded (likelihood: high)
Solenoid coil open (likelihood: medium)
Harness damaged (likelihood: medium)
Engine module driver faulty (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0805 - Clutch Position Sensor A Circuit

title: DTC P0810 - Clutch Position Control Error

title: DTC P0812 - Reverse Input Circuit

title: DTC P0815 - Upshift Switch Circuit

No manufacturer document with P081F is available to us; a GM service update for the 2016 Malibu and 2016–17 Volt explains the part and the 'won't shift out of park' complaint. title: DTC P0825 - Gear Lever Push-Pull Switch (Shift Anticipate)
problem_description: P0825 concerns a switch on the selector that reports pushing or pulling the lever – sequential + and – shifting – or the start of a shift movement, hence 'shift anticipate'. problem_description: Neutral position sensor A is a position sensor, usually a three-wire Hall sensor, on the shift shaft of a manual gearbox. Audi uses it as sender G701 on Q3 and A3, GM on the 2019 Corvette ZR1 with its 7-speed manual, where these codes suspend the gear ratio checks. Audi's bulletin for the sister codes P086D/P086E found the supply wires to G701 too short and lengthened them. Start-stop stays off.

Warning about the start system
MIL possible depending on maker

Sensor faulty (likelihood: medium)

Supply output of the control module (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: neutral position sensor, sensor wiring, engine control module, manual transmission.

title: DTC P0961 - Pressure Control Solenoid A Control Circuit Range/Performance
problem_description: Performance fault of pressure control solenoid A: the circuit is electrically intact, but the solenoid does not behave as commanded. On GM's six-speeds, where A is the line pressure solenoid, the Saab 9-4X 6T70 sets it when measured and commanded current differ for 5 s, GM's 2018 table after 4.4 of 5 s; both Type B, two trips. GM checks both states: in the 2016 HPC2 table P0A0D sets when the sensed voltage exceeds 24 % of 5 V with the source switched off (5 of 8 samples) or 44 % with it switched on (4 of 6 samples), Type A with MIL after one trip. Hyundai's Sonata Hybrid 2011-2015 bulletins send P0A0D straight to the HEV safety plug, alongside high-voltage path and relay codes, with check engine light and no ready mode. Mercedes model line 243 stores P0A0D00 in the battery management as a short to positive. P0A0C is the low-side counterpart; both leave the HV system switched off.
symptoms: No ready mode or ready light blinking
Check engine and charging warning lights on
Vehicle cannot be started
possible_causes: Service/safety plug not fully inserted or with poor contact (Hyundai Sonata Hybrid) (likelihood: high)
Interlock wire shorted to a 12 V or reference voltage (likelihood: medium)
Damaged interlock harness or connector after body or battery work (likelihood: medium)
Faulty interlock stage in the battery or hybrid control module (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0A0D (High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: hv interlock loop, hv service connector.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-4 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Service/safety plug not fully inserted or with poor contact (Hyundai Sonata Hybrid) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Interlock wire shorted to a 12 V or reference voltage (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P0A0E - High Voltage System Interlock Circuit A Intermittent
problem_description: The interlock loop A signal drops out or jumps for short moments and then recovers, so the module sees an unstable loop rather than a lasting open or short. Typical are connectors with loose or spread contacts, harness sections that move with the body or drivetrain, and moisture in seals. No manufacturer documents P0A0E publicly; the GM tables only list P0A0C and P0A0D for the same loop. Reference designs and patents on interlock monitoring describe the loop as a current or voltage path through each HV connector and point out that contact resistance and interference can cause brief false trips. CARB treats the HVIL as a safety-only system. For the driver this means sudden HV shutdowns or no-starts that come and go; static faults use P0A0A to P0A0D.
symptoms: Hybrid/EV warning that appears and disappears
Occasional loss of ready mode or sudden shutdown of electric drive
Intermittent no-start, often after rough roads or rain
possible_causes: Loose or spread interlock contacts in an HV or low-voltage connector (likelihood: high)
Harness section with a broken strand that opens under vibration (likelihood: medium)
Moisture entering through a damaged connector seal (likelihood: medium)
Electrical interference on the interlock line or a weak module input (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: hv interlock circuit a, wiring harness, bms.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-6 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Loose or spread interlock contacts in an HV or low-voltage connector (likelihood: high).

title: DTC P0A0F - Engine Failed to Start
problem_description: The control module commanded an engine start – by the hybrid system or an automatic start/stop restart – but the combustion engine did not reach a self-sustaining run within the allowed attempts. The code describes the result, not the cause. Toyota sets P0A0F with MIL on the 2010-2013 Prius and Prius v when a separated purge VSV/PCV hose leans out the mixture, often with P3190, P3191 and P0171. Kia traced P0A0F on the 2017-2018 Niro hybrid to an A/C pressure sensor harness chafed by an idler pulley, which disturbs the engine ECU 5 V reference. Audi sets P0A0F00 on 2019 A6/A7 3.0 mild hybrids after the second failed automatic restart, with a drive system warning. Look at fuel, air, ignition and engine sensor faults first.

Engine does not start, or runs briefly and stops
Reduced power because the vehicle runs on the battery only

title: DTC P0A10 - DC/DC Converter Status Circuit High
problem_description: The status signal from the DC/DC converter to the hybrid control module sits above its valid range, typically because the line is shorted to a voltage source, its ground or pull-down path is open, or the converter drives the output high after an internal failure. The converter supplies the 12 V system from the traction battery, and its self-diagnosis reports problems over this status path. No manufacturer documents P0A10 publicly in an official source; older lists that call it a hybrid battery voltage sense circuit are wrong for today's J2012. Siblings: P0A08 is the general status fault, P0A09 the low signal. A converter that stops working shows up as warning lights and a falling 12 V voltage until the hybrid system shuts down.

title: DTC P0A11 - DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit/Open
problem_description: General or open-circuit fault on the enable line with which the hybrid or battery control module tells the DC/DC converter that it may deliver power to the 12 V system. In typical designs a high enable level permits converter output, and a CAN message carries the same permission in parallel, so the two can be cross-checked. If the line is open, the converter cannot be switched on reliably and the 12 V battery is no longer charged. No manufacturer documents P0A11 publicly in an official source; Honda's hybrid recall shows what follows when the converter shuts down: charging warning, discharged 12 V battery, possible loss of drive. Low and high faults on the same line are P0A12 and P0A13; status line faults are P0A08 to P0A10.

Vehicle may lose motive power after a while

Faulty enable output driver in the control module (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0A12 - DC/DC Converter Enable Circuit Low
problem_description: The enable line to the DC/DC converter reads low when the control module is commanding it on. Because a low enable level usually means converter output is not permitted, the converter stays off and the 12 V system loses its charging source. Typical causes are a short to ground on the enable wire, a weak output driver in the module, or an input stage in the converter that loads the line. Older lists name this code DC/DC converter communication; today's J2012 wording is enable circuit low. No manufacturer documents P0A12 publicly in an official source, so the description rests on CARB and on patent descriptions of hard-wired enable lines. P0A11 covers an open line, P0A13 a line stuck high. Drivers see a charging warning and a draining 12 V battery.

12 V voltage drops, electrical consumers misbehave
Hybrid system may shut down when the 12 V battery is flat

Converter enable input internally shorted (likelihood: low)

title: DTC P0A14 - Engine Mount A Control Circuit/Open
problem_description: Some vehicles use switchable or active engine mounts that the powertrain or a mount control unit changes between soft and firm, or drives with an actuator against vibration. P0A14 reports an open or undefined fault in the control circuit of mount A. Ford lists it in its 2020 to 2023 gasoline OBD summary as the active mount circuit check: the low-side driver reports the fault and it matures after about 5 seconds; mount B uses P0AB6 to P0AB8. Honda's active control engine mounts, for example on the 2008 Pilot V6, use P0A14 for the front mount actuator and P0AB6 for the rear. P0A15 and P0A16 cover low and high faults. The car stays drivable, but vibration may increase.

title: DTC P0A17 - Motor Torque Sensor Circuit
problem_description: Some electric drive units measure the torque on the motor or generator shaft directly, for example with a magnetostrictive sensor inside a hollow motor shaft as described in Honda patents for hybrid drive systems. The control unit uses that value to check the torque it commands. P0A17 is the general circuit fault of this sensor, set when the signal is missing or cannot be evaluated at all. No manufacturer documents P0A17 publicly. CARB requires a monitoring plan for drive motor faults that affect propulsion or emission strategies, which covers such feedback sensors. Plausibility is P0A18, low and high P0A19 and P0A20, intermittent P0A21. Expect reduced electric power and a hybrid warning.

title: DTC P0A84 - Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit Low

GM tests it while the fan is commanded at low duty: a circuit voltage below about 0.26 V counts as a failure, and 16 fails in 20 samples at 250 ms set a Type B code (MIL after two trips). Another GM hybrid program detects it through the output stage status flag (20 of 25 samples). Mitsubishi lists P0A84 in the BMU and PHEV ECU of the 2018–20 Outlander PHEV among codes caused by a frozen battery heater relay, so meaning can differ by maker. Open and high faults are P0A81 and P0A85. With the output pulled low the fan may not respond, the pack warms up and power can be reduced.
symptoms: Check engine or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan does not follow commands
Reduced hybrid power when the pack gets warm
possible_causes: Fan control wire chafed and shorted to ground (likelihood: high)
Internal short in the fan's control input (likelihood: medium)
Moisture or corrosion in the fan connector (likelihood: low)
Defective output stage in the controller (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0A84 (Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit Low).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: battery cooling fan, wiring harness, bms.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Fan control wire chafed and shorted to ground (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Internal short in the fan's control input (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard

title: DTC P0A86 - 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit
problem_description: The 14 volt power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network of a hybrid or electric vehicle from the high-voltage battery; GM calls it the Accessory Power Module (APM). Current sensor A measures the current flowing through this converter. P0A86 is the general circuit code for that sensor, used when the controller recognises a fault in the sensor circuit without classifying it as low, high, implausible or intermittent (P0A87 to P0A8A). No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's published tables for the same APM input sensor use only the low/high codes P0A88 and P0A89. With an untrustworthy current reading the hybrid controller may limit or switch off the converter, so the 12 V battery can run down over time.

Possibly no other noticeable change in driving

title: DTC P0A87 - 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
problem_description: This code means the current sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter, GM: APM) delivers values that are electrically valid but implausible. GM's 2016 eAssist tables (hybrid control processor HPC1) describe a stuck-in-range test: once per key cycle, while the high-voltage contactors are open and then move to precharge, the converter should be off, so the averaged input current must be near zero. If the average is 0.50 A or more, P0A87 sets as a Type B code, so the MIL comes on after two failed trips. The test is skipped while P0A88 or P0A89 is active. Unlike those circuit low/high codes, the wiring is usually intact here; a sensor with offset drift is the typical finding.

Usually no driveability change
Possible reduced 12 V charging if the converter is limited
possible_causes: Current sensor zero-point drift inside the power module (likelihood: high)
Converter actually conducting current when it should be off (internal module fault) (likelihood: medium)
Ground or reference fault distorting the sensor signal (likelihood: low)

Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

title: DTC P0A89 - 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit High

title: DTC P0A8D - 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage Low

title: DTC P0A93 - Inverter A Cooling System Performance
problem_description: The power inverter of a hybrid has its own coolant circuit with an electric pump, radiator and fan, separate from engine cooling. P0A93 is set when this circuit does not cool as intended. CARB lists inverter thermal management among the components that hybrid OBD must monitor. Hyundai documents the code for the 2011 Sonata Hybrid (bulletin 14-HC-001), assigning it, like P0C73, to the electric water pump; symptoms include a hybrid warning, no EV mode and poor acceleration. Toyota recalled 2004–2009 Prius models (12V-536) because the inverter water pump could fail and cause a stall; that notice does not name a code. A leaking or air-locked circuit should also be checked.

No EV mode, reduced power
Vehicle may not start or may stall

title: DTC P0AA2 - Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
problem_description: P0AA2 means the positive main contactor does not close, or does not conduct, when the controller commands it closed, so the high-voltage bus cannot be energised from the pack. Audi traces rare cases to oxidised contact surfaces in the battery junction box after long standing or high humidity, and first prescribes repeated ignition cycles and an EV road test before replacing the junction box. GM lists the code among high-voltage faults for which Ultium EV pack data must be collected. Unlike P0AA1, the contacts are open, not welded.

title: DTC P0AD0 - Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Performance/Stuck Off
problem_description: P0AD0 is a functional fault: the control line of battery fan 3 may be electrically fine, but the blower does not deliver what was commanded, or stays still. Depending on design, the controller compares fan speed feedback with the request, or, as a Honda patent describes, compares the expected battery temperature change for the known cooling capacity with the measured one. CARB asks for such a functional check of the battery cooling where feasible. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD0 itself; circuit faults of the same fan are P0ACF, P0AD2 and P0AD3, the opposite case is P0AD1. The driver usually sees a hybrid warning and reduced power on hot days.

Subaru documents it on the 2014-15 XV Crosstrek Hybrid (bulletin 16-94-15R), together with P172A: a leaking O-ring at the electric oil pump relief valve can let CVT fluid into the pump motor. The check removes the three U, V and W cables at the oil pump inverter and reads AC voltage across them with the engine held at 1800 rpm in Park; 0.5 V or more means the drive motor and case assembly with the damaged seal must be replaced, less means the cause lies elsewhere. Subaru adds that P0C79, drive motor inverter voltage too high, appears only together with these codes and does not mean the inverter is faulty. P0B09 and P0B0A are the open and low variants.
symptoms: Warning lamp on, hybrid or CVT function restricted
Possibly P0C79 stored at the same time
possible_causes: CVT fluid entering the pump motor via a leaking relief valve O-ring (Subaru XV Crosstrek Hybrid) (likelihood: high)
Supply circuit shorted to a higher voltage source (likelihood: medium)
Oil pump inverter or its voltage sensing faulty (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code P0B0B (Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Supply Voltage Circuit High).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: aux trans pump a motor, wiring harness, tcm.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-12 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: CVT fluid entering the pump motor via a leaking relief valve O-ring (Subaru XV Crosstrek Hybrid) (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Supply circuit shorted to a higher voltage source (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

title: DTC P0B0C - Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Hydraulic Leakage
problem_description: P0B0C says the circuit fed by auxiliary pump A loses pressure through a leak, so the pump cannot hold the demanded pressure. Stellantis documents it as P0B0C 7A for the 2023-26 Jeep Avenger and 2026 Compass with hybrid dual-clutch transmission outside the US (TSB 21-061-26): an internal leak at the parking pawl locking piston causes jerking and power loss and may stop the engine from restarting after a stop; with P07E4 or P07E6 present and more than 5 km on the clock, the piston or the transmission is replaced. How a controller can see a leak shows a Nidec patent: after a speed change the pump current keeps falling instead of recovering, and the pump is stopped. P0B0B and P0B09 cover the supply, P2797 a pump that does not deliver.

Engine fails to restart after a stop
Transmission warning, possibly with P07E4 or P07E6

title: DTC P0B0D - Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Motor Control Module

U0287 is lost communication with the pump module, P0C23 to P0C25 its circuit.

title: DTC P0B0E - Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit
problem_description: Many packs measure current with two channels or two sensors so the controller can cross-check them; sensor B is the second channel next to sensor A (P0ABF to P0AC3). P0B0E is its general circuit code. Toyota uses it as the base of internal codes on the 2020-25 RAV4 Hybrid: the sensor sends a voltage rising with current on channel IB0 (sensor A) and an inverse one on IB1 (sensor B). P0B0E11 (IB1 too low) and P0B0E15 (IB1 too high or open) are reported to a generic scan tool as P0B10 and P0B11, one trip, MIL on. GM monitors its fine-range channel B with P0B10, P0B11 and the A/B correlation P0B13. CARB requires circuit monitoring. State of charge then becomes uncertain.

title: DTC P0B0F - Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
problem_description: P0B0F flags a current sensor B signal that is electrically in range but implausible, for example an offset at zero current or a value that does not match the other measurement. title: DTC P0C46 - Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

title: DTC P0C4E - Drive Motor A Position Exceeded Learning Limit

title: DTC P0C60 - Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit B Range/Performance
problem_description: P0C60 indicates that the second winding of the motor B resolver (Circuit B) is electrically intact but delivers values the controller rejects as unrealistic, for example an amplitude that no longer agrees with the first winding or an angle that jumps against the measured speed. title: DTC P0C75 - Hybrid/EV Battery System Discharge Time Too Short
problem_description: P0C75 is logged when the high-voltage bus loses its voltage faster than expected after the contactors open. At shutdown the inverter's DC-link capacitor is drained through a discharge resistor or an active discharge circuit, and from capacitance and resistance the controller knows roughly how long that should take. A capacitor diagnostic patent (EP2682769B1) uses the same comparison to detect capacitor ageing. No manufacturer documents P0C75 publicly; GM publishes only the opposite check, P0C76. The driver usually sees a hybrid warning lamp, and depending on the make the next start may be blocked.

title: DTC P0C7C - Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor G Circuit
problem_description: P0C7C is the umbrella circuit code for battery temperature sensor G, used when the controller sees an electrical fault in that input without sorting it into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P0C7C publicly. GM numbers sensor G as sensor 7 of the nine thermistors in the Volt pack (bulletin 18-NA-342), yet its hybrid tables only carry the narrower codes P0C7D to P0C80; Mitsubishi likewise splits sensor G into rationality, short and open. CARB section (e)(15.3.1) asks for continuous checks of range and circuit continuity on every such input. Without a trustworthy reading the battery controller has to assume the worst for that cell group and trims charge and discharge power. The thermistor lives inside the high-voltage pack, so testing needs HV safety procedures.

title: DTC P0CBF - Drive Motor A Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit High
problem_description: P0CBF is the code for an excessive signal from the coolant temperature sensor of drive motor A. title: DTC P0CC5 - 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A/B Correlation
problem_description: P0CC5 compares the two current sensors of the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C, where the unit is the accessory power module (APM), sensor A measures the input and sensor B the output side. The module computes an input power, multiplies it by an efficiency factor taken from a table (0.99 down to 0.90) and compares the result with the power derived from the output side; a gap above 0.4 kW for 3.75 s within a 5 s window, at 9 to 32 V and with the input power inside the enabling window the table ties to 1.25 kW, is a Type B fault. The check is suspended while the single-sensor codes P0A88/P0A89 or P0C9E/P0C9F are active. One drifting sensor is the usual reason, and a 12 V battery that stays poorly charged is a typical sign.
symptoms: Check-engine lamp after the second faulty trip
12 V battery not fully charged or low-voltage warning
possible_causes: Offset or gain drift of one current sensor (likelihood: high)
Internal fault of the power module, e.g. real efficiency loss (likelihood: medium)

title: DTC P0CD7 - Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

title: DTC P0CDA - Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit C
problem_description: P0CDA belongs to the rotor position sensor of drive motor A, normally a resolver: an excited stator winding induces signals in pick-up windings so the motor controller can work out rotor angle and speed. title: DTC P0CF3 - Control Pilot Circuit/Open

title: DTC P0CF8 - Control Pilot Charging Switch A Circuit/Open

title: DTC P0D00 - Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Circuit/Open
problem_description: Some battery types can give off gases while charging; for that case the conductive charging standards provide a state in which the vehicle asks the station for ventilation. title: DTC P0D1C - Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Stuck On

Coolant then keeps flowing through the wrong path, so the pack may be overcooled or heated poorly. The opposite fault is P0D1B.

title: DTC P0D32 - DC/DC Converter A Over Temperature
problem_description: P0D32 means DC/DC converter A, which supplies the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery, has become too hot. Unlike the sensor codes P0C38-P0C3C, the reading itself is trusted; the temperature is the problem. Honda names P0D32 in bulletin 26-025 for 2023-2025 Accord Hybrid models alongside other power control unit overheating codes such as P0A3C and P0A3E: road debris can get past a weak guard and damage the PCU radiator, coolant escapes, and several warning lights appear with reduced hybrid performance. The remedy is a new guard and, if the radiator leaks, a new radiator. Low coolant, a weak electronics coolant pump, a clogged radiator or trapped air are the usual causes. title: DTC P0D34 - Hybrid/EV Battery System Current
problem_description: P0D34 is the general code for the current flowing through the high-voltage battery system as a whole. No manufacturer publishes this code; GM's Volt and ELR charger module measures the same current but reports only low and high readings (P0D49, P0D4A), with 54 A as its upper limit. Range and sporadic faults have the codes P0D48 and P0D4B. The Ford patent on a DC/DC stage housed in the charger describes such a unit feeding the 12 V bus whenever the car is connected to a charging station. Under CARB rules every input of this kind must be checked for circuit faults. Without a valid current value the charger cannot limit its auxiliary output, so it may switch that stage off.
symptoms: 12 V battery discharges during long charging sessions
Charging may be interrupted
possible_causes: Open or shorted current sense circuit of the low-voltage stage (likelihood: medium)
Failed on-board charger electronics (likelihood: medium)
Damaged 12 V output connector at the charger (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: battery charger 14v output current sensor, wiring harness, on board charger.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

title: DTC P0D48 - Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
problem_description: P0D48 marks a current reading at the charger's 14 V output that lies within its electrical range but makes no sense in context. No manufacturer documents P0D48. GM covers a related check differently: its Volt and ELR charger module multiplies the 14 V output voltage by the current and sets P0D5B when this low-voltage power exceeds a limit derived from the measured AC input power plus 125 W. CARB defines a rationality diagnostic as comparing a sensor with all other available information, which is exactly what this code represents. Suspects are drift in the charger's sense circuit or its software; repair normally means reprogramming or replacing the charger.

title: DTC P0DAB - Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Performance
problem_description: P0DAB is the overall verdict on cell balancing: the battery controller sees that bleeding charge off the fuller cells no longer brings the pack back into line, so the spread between cells stays too wide. Toshiba's patent US20130026994A1 lists an open balancing terminal as one of the faults a monitoring chip should report, and this is the typical root of a stuck-off result. Because no charge is taken away from the high cells in group D, the pack's top end is governed by them; the charger and the controller stop earlier and the displayed range creeps down. The fault rarely causes a sudden breakdown. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires balancing to stay functional. Ford uses P0DBA in its hybrid BECM (OBD summary 2015); the stuck-off decision comes from comparing the six cells of circuit D with the pack average at power-up, 75 mV being the limit. The always-on opposite is P0DB9, the overall verdict P0DAB.
symptoms: MIL and battery warning
Range slowly decreasing, charging finishing early
possible_causes: Open balancing terminal or cell tap in group D (likelihood: high)
Bleed resistor of circuit D open (likelihood: medium)
Balancing transistor of circuit D failed open (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: hv battery cell balancing circuit d, bms.

Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.

title: DTC P0DBB - Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D Range/Performance

A clear reference is GM's eAssist key-off test for a related code: engaging the bleed load has to pull the cell at least 0.1 V away from its rest value. A result outside the expected window, even with intact wiring, is what a performance code captures. Passive balancing turns excess charge into heat, as the Wikipedia article on battery balancing outlines, so a weak resistor or a cell with changed internal resistance shifts the outcome. title: DTC P0DBD - Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E Stuck On
