title: DTC U0488 - Invalid Data Received From Digital Disc Player/Changer Module A
problem_description: U0488 is logged when the first networked disc drive, module A, still reports on the bus but its data fail the receiver's checks; U0187 would mean the drive is silent, while U0489, U048A and U0491 cover drives B to D. Many GM vehicles of 2013-2015 carried such a separate media disc player with its own fuse: bulletin PIT5344B (ATS, Escalade, Silverado, Tahoe and others) told technicians to cycle that fuse when CD playback stopped and to replace the player only if power and ground tested fine. In optical MOST networks a drive of this kind is a ring member that streams its audio to the head unit. No manufacturer documents U0488 itself. The radio then refuses disc playback while other sources keep working; no MIL.

title: DTC U0499 - Invalid Data Received From Telematic Control Module

title: DTC U04BA - Invalid Data Received From Switch Input Module A
problem_description: A switch input module collects the positions of several buttons and reports them to other control units as network frames. U04BA means that frames from module A keep arriving, but the receiver, usually the body controller, rejects their content: a switch state outside the defined values, a wrong message counter, a failed checksum or an unexpected length. An Eaton patent describes such a module in which a controller polls each switch address and acts only on replies carrying a valid address and state. Which buttons belong to module A is up to the carmaker; no maker documents this code publicly. If module A falls silent, U01B7 is set instead. For the driver, the buttons handled by this module may do nothing or trigger the wrong function.

title: DTC U04BB - Invalid Data Received From Switch Input Module B
problem_description: U04BB concerns the second switch input module. title: DTC U04BC - Invalid Data Received From Switch Input Module C
problem_description: With a third switch input module, addressing becomes a weak point. Several near-identical switch units often hang on one LIN line as slaves, and each needs its own node address, assigned either by part variant or by an auto-addressing routine at start-up. If two units end up with the same address, or a reply arrives with a bad LIN checksum, the master receives data it cannot assign and the controller records U04BC for module C. Nothing public ties this code to a specific make or to a fixed location in the car. U01B9 covers the case where module C does not answer at all, and U04BD, which follows in the list, belongs to the park lock module rather than to this series. On a car with four side doors, A to D would already be enough for one unit per door, so E suggests an additional switch location; no manufacturer documents this code or says what E means. Rear or sliding doors with their own electronics are plausible candidates: Yazaki's patent US8304928 describes doors with dedicated controllers, each serving a window switch module, joined to the body network through a LIN sub-bus. One interaction matters for any rear switch: the driver's window lockout blocks rear requests deliberately, so a rear switch that does nothing is not by itself a fault. The code becomes meaningful when frames from unit E contain implausible values; U0219 indicates the unit has gone silent.
symptoms: Switch at an additional door position without function
Window at that position operable only from the driver's door
possible_causes: Switch unit E internally faulty or water-damaged (likelihood: medium)
Fault on the LIN sub-bus wiring between door controller and switch (likelihood: medium)
Switch variant not matching the vehicle configuration (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: door switch e.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: DIY feasible. Estimated labor time: 0.3-1.5 hours

title: DTC U0521 - Invalid Data Received From Door Switch F
problem_description: Door switch unit F lies beyond the usual four side doors. title: DTC U0522 - Invalid Data Received From Door Switch G
problem_description: J2012 provides seven door switch units, and G is the last of them. Few vehicles need that many networked switch packs, and no manufacturer publishes what G stands for or documents U0522. Where such a unit exists it works like its siblings: it supplies its button states when asked, and the receiver ignores them once a frame is malformed, out of range or carries an invalid counter. After a switch pack has been replaced or the body controller reconfigured, a variant or software level that does not suit the vehicle can produce exactly this pattern; FCA's Cherokee bulletin 08-013-15 shows door-switch codes being cleared by BCM software and a restored configuration. title: DTC U0523 - Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor A
problem_description: A door window motor in the J2012 sense is a lift motor with its own electronics that talks to the network, usually as a LIN slave of a door or body controller. Such a unit reports where the glass is, based on its Hall pulses, whether it stopped for an obstacle or a stall and whether its sensor or supply has failed, as NXP's MM908E624 reference design (AN3147) shows. U0523 is stored when these reports from motor A reach the master but cannot be used. No manufacturer documents the code or the door behind letter A. Typical consequences are a window that only moves while the switch is held, a missing express function or no automatic closing on locking. Lost communication with the same motor is U0222.

title: DTC U0524 - Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor B
problem_description: U0524 means the master accepts frames from window motor B but not what they say. A common reason is a position value the controller cannot reconcile. Smart lift motors count Hall pulses between a learned lower and upper end, and Atmel's anti-pinch application note AVR480 describes acquiring such parameters during initialisation and spotting a defective Hall sensor from a run of apparent direction changes. After a battery disconnection, a motor replacement or a regulator that has slipped, the stored travel no longer matches reality, and many systems fall back to manual operation until the window has been re-initialised. No manufacturer publishes setting criteria for U0524 or the door assigned to B. U0223 covers a motor that has stopped answering.

title: DTC U0525 - Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor C
problem_description: Data from window motor C include what the door controller needs for automatic closing, which in the United States falls under FMVSS 118. A window able to close without the switch being held must stop and reverse before it presses on a test rod of 4 to 200 mm with 100 N or more, and then open again by at least 125 mm or far enough for a 200 mm rod. If the reports from motor C are corrupt, the controller can no longer rely on that reversal, so a cautious design blocks one-touch and remote closing for this window. No manufacturer documents U0525 or names the door behind C. Raising and lowering with the switch held usually still works; U0224 is the lost-communication partner.

title: DTC U0526 - Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor D
problem_description: Not every lift motor carries Hall sensors. Patent US11611297 describes a cheaper approach in which the controller derives speed, current and how quickly current changes from the ripple that commutation leaves in the motor current, and recognises a pinch from those values. Positions obtained this way are sensitive to supply noise and brush wear, so the data reported by window motor D may drift out of the plausible range and lead to U0526. No manufacturer publishes this code or says which door uses letter D. Practical effects resemble the sister codes: express and comfort closing disabled, a lost end position, sometimes a window that halts part way. U0225 is stored instead when motor D does not answer at all.

problem_description: Window motor F is one of the slots beyond the four usual side doors; it could serve, for instance, powered rear quarter glass or a sliding door window, but no manufacturer documents which window F stands for or publishes U0528. title: DTC U052A - Invalid Data Received From Heated Steering Wheel Module
problem_description: The heated steering wheel module powers the heating mat in the rim and reports its state, such as heater on or off, the requested level and the rim temperature read by an embedded thermistor, to the body or climate network. A receiver that gets these frames but finds the content implausible (temperature out of range, bad checksum or counter, wrong length) logs U052A; if the frames stop entirely, U0229 is set instead. Ford shows that the hardware depends on the option: if adaptive steering is fitted, heating is a job of Ford's SECM, the steering effort controller inside the wheel, otherwise of a separate HSWM (SSM 47850). title: DTC U0530 - Invalid Data Received From Object Detection Maintenance Control Module B
problem_description: Module B of this family is a second maintenance controller for object detection sensors, for instance one serving another sensor group or the other side of the vehicle. The generic definition offers no public explanation, and no manufacturer document names U0530. Denso's patent US11451765 illustrates the kind of decision such a unit supports: two sensors sharing a field of view are compared, and when they disagree about the objects they see, one of them is judged dirty and marked for cleaning. problem_description: U0573 is the B variant: invalid data from a second vehicle motion control module. A second unit makes sense where coordination tasks are split, for example lateral and longitudinal motion, or where a backup must take over for automated driving. Hitachi Astemo's patent explains why timing matters in such systems: actuator modules receive their instructions over a shared network that also carries other traffic, so each instruction refers to a common time frame. Data from B that arrive outside that frame, with stale counters or with values contradicting module A are rejected and stored as U0573. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, and no lost-communication code exists for this module. Coordinated functions are then reduced.

title: DTC U0619 - Lost Communication With Reductant Level Sensor A
problem_description: Reductant level sensor A reports how much diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) is left in the SCR tank. Newer tank units are smart sensors: a sensing element plus electronics that transmit level, temperature and often concentration as digital frames over CAN, SENT or LIN. U0619 means the engine or aftertreatment controller gets no valid frames from that level sensor, whether the line is silent, frames time out, checksums fail or the sensor flags an internal fault. CARB requires a digital input that stops talking to store its own code, apart from the circuit and plausibility codes P203A to P203E. No manufacturer publicly documents a detection rule for U0619. Without a level value the low-DEF warning is lost and the controller can no longer rule out an empty tank, which California treats as an SCR fault.

No warning before the DEF tank runs empty

Electronics of the tank level sensor failed (often replaced as a tank sender unit) (likelihood: medium)
Controller software or configuration not matching the installed sensor (likelihood: low)

title: DTC U061E - Lost Communication With Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Module
problem_description: A battery isolation or voltage stabilization module separates a second 12 V battery or protected loads from the starter circuit, so that cranking during an automatic restart does not drag the voltage of the rest of the vehicle down. title: DTC U061F - Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 1 Sensor 1

title: DTC U0625 - Lost Communication With Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Bank 1

title: DTC U0666 - Lost Communication With Reductant Pressure Sensor
problem_description: The reductant pressure sensor watches the DEF line between the supply pump and the dosing valve. Bosch, for instance, offers its supply module with or without such a sensor; with it, the pump only runs when dosing is requested, the line stays pressurised through stop-start phases and is purged at key-off against freezing. If the sensor speaks a digital protocol, U0666 means its messages have stopped reaching the controller. No manufacturer documents this code in public. CARB places each SCR sensor under its comprehensive component rules and demands both a dedicated code for a silent digital input and detection of faulty reductant delivery. Analog faults are P204A to P204E, pressure too low or high P20E8 or P20E9. Dosing usually stops, followed by DEF warnings and possibly a MIL.

title: DTC U0675 - Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A
problem_description: A speed sensor in the bearing or compressor housing lets the controller watch how fast the turbocharger rotor spins, mainly to keep it below its overspeed limit; a BorgWarner patent (US9353760B2) describes such a sensor and gives that reason, and CARB names turbocharger/turbine speed among the data diesel vehicles must output. Classic sensors send a pulse train whose faults are P2578 to P2582. U0675 applies when sensor A delivers the speed as a digital message and those messages are missing or invalid. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Without a speed value the controller cannot tell how close the rotor is to its limit, so it will usually cap boost and engine power until the fault is gone.
symptoms: Check engine light
Boost and power limited
Noticeably weaker acceleration at higher loads
possible_causes: Sensor wiring near the turbocharger heat-damaged or broken (likelihood: high)
Connector loose, oily or corroded (likelihood: medium)
Speed sensor electronics failed (likelihood: medium)
Engine controller input or software fault (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U0675 (Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: turbo speed sensor a, vehicle bus wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-2.5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Sensor wiring near the turbocharger heat-damaged or broken (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: Connector loose, oily or corroded (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.

title: DTC U0676 - Lost Communication With Fuel Level Sensor A
problem_description: Fuel level sensor A is the main tank sender. Usually it is a float-driven resistor read as a voltage, and U0676 only applies where the sender itself reports digitally and its messages stop. Public documentation of this code from any manufacturer is lacking. In its 2024 summary Ford treats sender A as a resistance: below 5 ohms or above 200 ohms within 30 s are circuit faults, more than 100 jumps of over 40 % are noise, and stuck checks need 100 to 120 miles. GM's 25OBDG03A lets the float feed the engine controller directly or a fuel tank zone module, which forwards the value, and pauses its range checks while a communication fault is active. CARB needs the level for EVAP testing and misfire disablement at low fuel, so the gauge may be wrong and those monitors stay incomplete.
symptoms: Fuel gauge reads empty, full or freezes
Range display missing or wrong
Check engine light, EVAP readiness not set
possible_causes: Wiring at the tank or fuel pump flange damaged or corroded (likelihood: high)
Electronics of the level sender failed (likelihood: medium)
Module that reads or forwards the level faulty (likelihood: medium)
Connector under the vehicle not latched or water-damaged (likelihood: low)

Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: fuel level sensor a, vehicle bus wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 0.5-3 hours

title: DTC U0677 - Lost Communication With Fuel Level Sensor B
problem_description: A second level sender is needed when a tank has two chambers, as in saddle tanks that straddle the driveshaft, or when a vehicle carries a second tank. title: DTC U067A - Lost Communication With Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch B
problem_description: Sensor B is the second pressure measuring point. In GM's 24OBDG07 B belongs to clutch 2, fed from its own reference VREF2, and Ford's 2024 summary checks TFP B with P0846 to P0848. U067A stands for a digital sensor B whose messages have stopped. problem_description: Parallel hybrids put a clutch between engine and electric motor so the car can drive electrically with the engine stopped. title: DTC U067D - Lost Communication With Fan 4

title: DTC U067F - Lost Communication With Barometric Pressure Sensor A

U067F covers a digital version of that sensor whose messages stop arriving. GM's dual-throttle program 23OBDG07 does read a digital ambient sensor, but files its faults under P-codes: a CRC error or a short reported in message A sets P2228 or P2229, and defect or queue-full flags set P2227, each after 2 s with MIL in one trip. Ford's 2024 gasoline and 2023 diesel summaries keep sensor A analog (P2228). No published table therefore assigns U067F. title: DTC U0680 - Lost Communication With Barometric Pressure Sensor B

U0680 is stored when the frames carrying the high and low line pressure of bank 2 come in with a wrong data length code for 1.5 s; the MIL follows after two trips. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM and Ford wire pedal E analog, with Ford setting P2127/P2128 on voltage limits and P2138 when D and E disagree by more than 0.9 degrees. title: DTC U0684 - Lost Communication With Catalyst Temperature Bank 1 Sensor 1
problem_description: A catalyst temperature sensor tells the controller when the converter is hot enough to work and to be tested. Sensor 1 on bank 1 is the first such probe on the bank that holds cylinder 1. U0684 applies when the probe sends its reading as a digital message and that message has stopped. The interlock is a low-voltage signal loop routed through the HV connectors and covers; the monitoring module drives a current or signal through it and opens the HV contactors, or refuses to close them, when the loop is broken or out of range, so that no HV connection can be opened while live.
symptoms: Vehicle will not switch to ready mode or the HV system shuts down
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
Charging may be blocked
possible_causes: Interlock wire shorted to ground (likelihood: high)
HV connector, service disconnect or cover switch not fully seated (likelihood: medium)
Damaged interlock wiring or corroded terminal in the loop (likelihood: medium)
Fault in the module that drives and evaluates the interlock loop (likelihood: low)
diagnostic_steps: Connect OBD-II diagnostic scanner and verify active code U351F (High Voltage System Interlock Circuit E Low).
Perform visual and physical inspection of affected components: hvil loop e, hvil wiring.
Check electrical wiring harnesses and connectors for looseness, corrosion, or pin displacement.
Measure reference voltage, ground continuity, and component resistance against manufacturer specifications.
Repair guidance: Professional technician service recommended. Estimated labor time: 1-5 hours
recommended_actions: Prioritize inspection of primary cause: Interlock wire shorted to ground (likelihood: high).
If issue persists, inspect secondary potential fault: HV connector, service disconnect or cover switch not fully seated (likelihood: medium).
Due to system criticality, have vehicle inspected by an ASE-certified technician.
source: OBDex / SAE J2012 & ISO 15031-6 Open Diagnostic Standard
preprocessing_notes: Ingested from U3xxx_enriched.yaml; standardized into vehicle troubleshooting schema.
